title: Blue Team — Defensive Security
description: Comprehensive defensive security curriculum covering detection engineering, incident response, threat hunting, and security operations.

modules.title: SIEM Foundations and Log Analysis
modules.objective: Navigate a SIEM platform, write search queries, and analyze Windows and Linux security logs to identify suspicious activity.

topics.title: SIEM Platform Architecture and Use Cases
concepts: What a SIEM does: centralized log aggregation, correlation, alerting, and dashboards
Major platforms: Splunk (Enterprise Security), Microsoft Sentinel (cloud-native, KQL), Elastic/ELK Stack (open-source, EQL/KQL), IBM QRadar (UCF correlation engine)
Data ingestion pipeline: forwarders → indexer/search head → dashboards/alerts
Parsing, normalization, and field extraction (Splunk props.conf/transforms.conf, Elastic ingest pipelines)
Licensing models: Splunk by ingest volume (GB/day), Sentinel by data retained + analytics, ELK self-hosted open-source
key_facts: Splunk Enterprise Security is the market leader but costs per GB of daily ingest
Microsoft Sentinel is fully cloud-native and uses Kusto Query Language (KQL) for all detection logic
Elastic Stack (ELK) is the primary open-source SIEM alternative
IBM QRadar uses a Universal Correlation Engine that normalizes all logs to QID mappings

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers attempt to operate below SIEM visibility by disabling logging (clearing Windows Security Event Log, stopping the Sysmon service), using living-off-the-land tools that blend into normal admin activity, or avoiding logs entirely with in-memory execution.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker encounters SIEM coverage they cannot disable, they experience a race condition — every action creates forensic artifacts. They must either blind the sensors (T1562 Impair Defenses) or move so quickly that detection and response cannot keep up (speed as defense bypass).
bypass_attempts: Clearing Windows Event Logs (Event ID 1102) to cover tracks
Stopping or disabling the Sysmon service (T1562.001)
Using legitimate admin tools (PowerShell, WMI) to blend with baseline activity
Injecting into trusted processes to avoid process-level logging

drills: Set up Splunk Free or Elastic and ingest Windows Security Event Logs — build a dashboard showing top 10 source IPs for Event ID 4625 (failed logons)
Compare Splunk SPL and Microsoft Sentinel KQL by writing equivalent queries for 'show all process creation events in the last 24 hours'
common_mistakes: Ingesting everything without filtering — leads to noise and excessive licensing costs (Splunk)
Not setting up proper field extraction at ingestion time, making searches slow and unreliable
Treating the SIEM as an archive rather than a detection engine

topics.title: Windows Security Event Log Analysis
concepts: Critical Security Event IDs: 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4688 (process creation), 4648 (explicit credential logon), 4672 (special privileges assigned), 4720 (account created), 4726 (account deleted), 4732 (member added to security group), 4738 (user account changed), 1102 (audit log cleared), 7045 (service installed in System log)

Logon types in Event 4624: Type 2 (Interactive), Type 3 (Network), Type 4 (Batch), Type 5 (Service), Type 7 (Unlock), Type 8 (NetworkCleartext), Type 9 (NewCredentials), Type 10 (RemoteInteractive/RDP), Type 11 (CachedInteractive)
Enabling advanced auditing via Group Policy: Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy
Command-line process auditing (Event 4688 with command line) requires enabling Audit Process Creation
key_facts: Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 3 (Network) from an unexpected internal host may indicate lateral movement
Event ID 4624 with Logon Type 10 indicates an RDP session — unusual for servers that should not have interactive users
Event ID 4720 (user account created) outside of normal IT provisioning hours is a high-signal indicator of attacker persistence
Event ID 1102 (audit log cleared) is itself a critical security event that should trigger immediate investigation
Event ID 7045 in System log (service installed) is critical for detecting attacker-installed services for persistence

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers create new accounts (Event 4720, T1136), use stolen credentials for lateral movement via SMB/RDP (Event 4624 Type 3/10, T1021), clear audit logs to cover tracks (Event 1102, T1070.001), and install services for persistence (Event 7045, T1543.003).
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker sees Windows as a rich logging environment that, if properly configured, records nearly every action. They must decide between speed (accept detection) and stealth (spend time disabling logs, which itself generates events). Clearing logs creates Event 1102 — an immediate red flag.
bypass_attempts: Using living-off-the-land binaries instead of custom malware to avoid process-creation anomalies
Clearing only specific event records rather than the entire log
Operating under context of legitimate service accounts to blend in with baseline activity

drills: In Splunk/Sentinel, write a query to detect Event ID 4720 (user creation) outside business hours, then correlate with subsequent 4624 logons by the new account
Build an alert for Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 (network logon) from a user who has never logged into that host before
common_mistakes: Only monitoring Event ID 4624 (successful logon) and ignoring 4625 patterns (brute-force detection)
Not enabling command-line logging (Event 4688) — missing critical context for process investigations
Focusing on individual events instead of correlating event sequences (e.g., 4720 followed by 4732 followed by 4624)

topics.title: Sysmon for Enhanced Endpoint Telemetry
concepts: Sysmon (System Monitor) is a free Sysinternals tool providing detailed process, network, and file telemetry beyond native Windows logging

Key Sysmon Event IDs: 1 (Process Creation with command line + parent process + hash), 3 (Network Connection), 7 (Image Loaded / DLL loaded), 8 (CreateRemoteThread — process injection indicator), 10 (Process Access — LSASS access detection), 11 (File Creation), 13 (Registry Value Set), 22 (DNS Query), 23 (File Delete Archived), 25 (Process Tampering)
Sysmon configuration via XML config file — defining include/exclude rules for process creation, network connections, file creations
Popular configurations: SwiftOnSecurity config (beginner), Olaf Hartong's sysmon-modular (advanced threat hunting)
Sysmon events go to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational event log channel
key_facts: Sysmon Event ID 1 provides full command-line, parent process, and process hash — more detail than native Event 4688
Sysmon Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) and Event ID 10 (Process Access with TargetImage containing lsass.exe) are key for detecting credential dumping (T1003.001)
Sysmon Event ID 7 (Image Loaded) detects DLL side-loading and injection via unsigned DLLs loaded into trusted processes
Sysmon Event ID 22 (DNS Query) enables detection of DNS-based C2 communication and data exfiltration
Sysmon is NOT an EDR — it has no prevention/blocking capability, only logging

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers dump LSASS memory for credentials (triggers Sysmon EID 10 with lsass.exe as TargetImage), inject code into remote processes (triggers Sysmon EID 8 CreateRemoteThread), create files for persistence (triggers Sysmon EID 11), register DNS lookups for C2 communication (triggers Sysmon EID 22).
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: An attacker on a Sysmon-monitored host realizes that every process spawn, network connection, file write, and DLL load is logged with rich metadata. The only ways to evade are: (1) operate entirely in memory without spawning processes (fileless), (2) tamper with the Sysmon service itself (EID 4 service state change), or (3) use a process already running with legitimate network connections.
bypass_attempts: Killing or stopping the Sysmon service (triggers EID 4/5 — itself a detection)
Using direct syscalls to avoid ETW and user-mode hooks that Sysmon relies on
Process doppelgänging to execute code from legitimate-looking process images
Blending into legitimate parent-child process trees (e.g., svchost.exe → powershell.exe)

drills: Deploy Sysmon with SwiftOnSecurity config on a lab VM. Trigger a simulated credential dump and identify the Sysmon Event ID 10 with lsass.exe access
Write a Splunk/Sentinel query for Sysmon EID 1 detecting suspicious parent-child relationships (e.g., winword.exe → cmd.exe or winword.exe → powershell.exe)
common_mistakes: Running Sysmon with default config (which captures almost nothing) instead of a curated configuration
Not ingesting Sysmon logs into the SIEM — collecting them locally but never centralizing
Generating too many events with overly broad config rules, creating a data volume and noise problem

topics.title: Splunk Search Processing Language (SPL)
concepts: SPL pipeline structure: search command | transforming commands | formatting commands
Core search syntax: index=main sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 | stats count by user, src_ip
Key commands: search, stats (aggregation), eval (field computation), where (filtering), table, chart, timechart, tstats (metadata acceleration), rex (regex extraction), lookup (enrichment)
Transaction command for correlating events across time (e.g., a full attack sequence)
Subsearches for complex correlations
key_facts: Use index= and sourcetype= at the start of every search for optimal performance
tstats is much faster than stats for indexed fields because it queries tsidx metadata files instead of raw events
Common SOC SPL pattern: index=* EventCode=4720 | stats count by Account_Name, ComputerName | sort -count
datamodel command enables CIM (Common Information Model) compliance for portable searches across data sources

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers execute discovery commands (whoami, net user, ipconfig, systeminfo) that get logged as process creations — the defender uses SPL to search for these command patterns across the environment.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: If the attacker's discovery commands are logged and searchable in Splunk, the defender can retroactively find the entire chain of attacker activity by pivoting from one suspicious event. The attacker cannot see what the defender searches, but any log they leave is a permanent forensic trail.
bypass_attempts: Using obfuscated or encoded commands to avoid SPL string matching
Operating via RDP or interactive sessions where commands aren't logged as process creation events
Clearing logs after discovery phase

drills: Write an SPL query to find all instances of PowerShell launching from Microsoft Office applications: index=main sourcetype=*sysmon* EventCode=1 ParentImage=*winword.exe Image=*powershell.exe
Use the transaction command to correlate a phishing email click with subsequent process execution and network connections within a 5-minute window
common_mistakes: Not restricting searches to specific indexes/sourcetypes, causing extremely slow searches
Using stats without proper groupby fields, producing meaningless aggregations
Over-relying on exact string matching instead of using wildcards or regex for flexibility

topics.title: Kusto Query Language (KQL) for Microsoft Sentinel
concepts: KQL syntax: tabular data model with pipe-delimited operators
Basic structure: SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4624 | summarize count() by Account, Computer
Key operators: where (filter), summarize (aggregation), project (select columns), join (correlate tables), extend (computed columns), parse (extract fields), make-series (time series)
Sentinel analytics rules: scheduled (KQL query on a schedule), Microsoft security (from other Microsoft products), fusion (ML-based correlation)
KQL for hunting: SecurityAlert | where Severity == 'High' | join kind=inner SecurityEvent on Computer
key_facts: KQL is read-only — it cannot modify data, only query and transform
Use '_GetWatchlist()' function to integrate threat intelligence watchlists into queries
Sentinel stores data in a Log Analytics workspace — retention and query costs are per-GB
KQL supports let statements for variable definition: let suspicious_users = SecurityEvent | where ... | distinct Account;

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers use stolen valid credentials (T1078) to authenticate — the defender uses KQL to detect anomalous logon patterns such as impossible travel, unusual logon hours, or first-time access to specific resources.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: An attacker using valid credentials looks legitimate in individual events. But when the defender correlates across time and geography using KQL, patterns emerge — a user logging in from New York and London within 30 minutes (impossible travel) is immediately suspicious.
bypass_attempts: Using VPNs or proxies that match the victim's typical geographic location
Logging in during the user's typical working hours to blend with baseline
Avoiding mass downloads or unusual access patterns that might trigger volume-based alerts

drills: Write a KQL query to detect impossible travel: SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4624 | summarize min(TimeGenerated), max(TimeGenerated), makeset(IPAddress) by Account | extend time_diff = datetime_diff('minute', max_TimeGenerated, min_TimeGenerated)
Build a Sentinel analytics rule for detecting first-time execution of PowerShell encoded commands on a host
common_mistakes: Writing KQL queries without time bounds, leading to full-workspace scans and slow performance
Not using summarize and project to reduce result set size before joining tables
Confusing KQL syntax with SQL — KQL uses pipe syntax, not SELECT/FROM/WHERE

topics.title: Elastic Security: KQL, EQL, and Kibana
concepts: Kibana Query Language (KQL): lightweight filter syntax for Elasticsearch documents, e.g., event.action:"process_started" and process.name:powershell.exe

Event Query Language (EQL): sequence-based detection for time-ordered events, e.g., sequence [process where process.name:"winword.exe"][process where process.name:"cmd.exe" and process.parent.name:"winword.exe"]
Elastic Security detection rules: pre-built rules from elastic/detection-rules repository, plus custom rules using KQL or EQL
Elastic Common Schema (ECS): standardized field naming (process.name, host.hostname, event.category) for cross-source normalization
Beats/Elastic Agent for data collection: Winlogbeat for Windows events, Packetbeat for network, Auditbeat for Linux
key_facts: EQL is powerful for detecting attack sequences — e.g., 'word document spawns PowerShell' as a parent-child process sequence
Elastic Security includes pre-built detection rules mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques
ECS (Elastic Common Schema) is the foundation — all data sources map to the same field names
Winlogbeat collects Windows Event Logs including Security, Application, System, Sysmon, and PowerShell operational logs

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers inject code into legitimate processes (T1055) to evade process-based detection — EQL sequence queries can still detect the anomalous parent-child relationships and thread creation patterns.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker encounters Elastic Security with well-tuned EQL rules, the sequence-based detection is hard to evade because it models the entire attack chain, not just individual events. Even if individual actions look benign, the sequence 'Office app → cmd.exe → network connection' is inherently suspicious.
bypass_attempts: Breaking the process chain by using process injection into unrelated running processes
Using WMI/DCOM for process execution instead of direct parent-child spawning
Operating via scheduled tasks where the parent process is the Task Scheduler service

drills: Write an EQL sequence query to detect credential dumping: any process accessing lsass.exe with suspicious access rights within a window after a suspicious process launch
Use KQL in Kibana Discover to filter for PowerShell ScriptBlock logging events containing encoded commands (base64 patterns)
common_mistakes: Confusing KQL (Kibana filter syntax) with EQL (event sequence language) — they serve different detection needs
Not mapping data sources to ECS before writing detection rules, leading to inconsistent field references
Using KQL for sequence-based detections when EQL is purpose-built for event correlation

modules.title: Detection Engineering and Detection-as-Code
modules.objective: Write, test, and deploy vendor-neutral detection rules using Sigma and YARA, and build a detection-as-code pipeline with version control and CI/CD.

topics.title: Sigma Rules — Vendor-Neutral Detection Format
concepts: Sigma is a generic, open YAML-based format for writing detection rules that can be converted to any SIEM's native query language
Sigma rule structure: title, id, status, description, author, date, logsource, detection (selection + condition), falsepositives, level, tags (including MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs)
logsource defines the data source: category (process_creation, network_connection, etc.), product (windows, linux), service
detection uses field modifiers: contains, startswith, endswith, all of them, 1 of selection*, regex
Sigma Converter (sigmac/pySigma) translates rules to Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL, Elastic EQL, QRadar AQL, and more
key_facts: Sigma is to detection rules what Snort/Suricata is to network IDS — a shared community standard
The SigmaHQ repository contains thousands of community-maintained rules on GitHub
Sigma tags follow MITRE ATT&CK: attack.t1003, attack.credential_access, attack.t1059.001
Rule levels: informational, low, medium, high, critical — maps to alert severity in the SOC
Sigma rules should focus on behavior, not specific tool names — detect the activity, not the malware

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers attempt credential dumping (T1003) using tools like mimikatz, procdump, or taskmgr to access LSASS memory. The Sigma rule detects the behavioral pattern — any process accessing lsass.exe with suspicious access rights (e.g., PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION).
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker cannot see the Sigma rules deployed by the defender. But when their LSASS access triggers an alert, they realize the defender has behavior-based detection, not just signature-based. This means renaming mimikatz.exe won't help — the detection targets the behavior of accessing lsass.exe, not the tool name.
bypass_attempts: Using indirect LSASS access via custom tools that don't match known tool signatures
Abusing legitimate diagnostic tools (procdump.exe from Sysinternals, Task Manager) that may be whitelisted
Reading LSASS via kernel-mode drivers that bypass user-mode hooks
Using DCSync to extract credentials from Active Directory instead of LSASS

drills: Write a Sigma rule detecting procdump.exe or mimikatz accessing lsass.exe (EID 10 TargetImage contains lsass.exe), then convert it to Splunk SPL and Sentinel KQL using sigmac
Browse the SigmaHQ repository and find 5 rules for detecting PowerShell encoded commands — analyze their detection logic
common_mistakes: Writing overly specific rules that break when the attacker renames a tool — focus on behavior, not tool name
Not using filters (falsepositives field) — rules that alert on every instance of a process are useless
Not testing converted rules — sigmac conversion can produce syntactically correct but logically broken SIEM queries

topics.title: YARA Rules — Malware Pattern Matching
concepts: YARA (Yet Another Recursive Acronym) is a pattern-matching tool for identifying and classifying malware based on textual or binary patterns
YARA rule structure: meta (metadata: description, author, date, reference), strings (text strings, hex strings, regex), condition (boolean logic referencing strings)
String types: $a = "text string", $b = { AA BB CC DD }, $c = /regex pattern/, $d = "wide ascii nocase"
Condition operators: and, or, not, of, any/all, filesize, pe.imports (for PE files), pe.imphash()
YARA scanning: on files, directories, memory dumps (via Volatility integration), or running processes
key_facts: YARA was created by Victor Alvarez (VirusTotal/Google) and is the de facto standard for malware family classification
YARA-X is the Rust-based rewrite offering faster scanning and better performance
The Neo23x0 YARA-Style-Guide is the community best-practice reference for writing maintainable rules
YARA rules can be integrated with EDR/AV products, SIEM platforms, and forensic tools for automated scanning
Common mistake: using overly broad strings that match legitimate software, causing massive false positives

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers deploy custom malware or modified known malware (obfuscated to evade signatures, T1027 Obfuscated Files). YARA rules detect malware families by matching characteristic code patterns, strings, or byte sequences even when the malware is partially modified.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker's malware is scanned by a YARA rule, the rule matches specific byte patterns or strings that the attacker may not know exist in their binary. Unlike hash-based detection, YARA catches modified/obfuscated versions because it targets structural patterns. The attacker must fundamentally alter their code's characteristics — not just rename or recompile — to evade YARA.
bypass_attempts: Polymorphic/metamorphic code that changes byte patterns on each compilation
String encryption — encrypting all identifiable strings and decrypting at runtime
Using packers/crypters (UPX, custom) to alter the binary structure
Living-off-the-land entirely (no custom malware) to avoid any YARA-matchable artifact

drills: Write a YARA rule to detect a known malware family by combining 3 unique strings with a condition: 2 of ($a, $b, $c) and filesize < 1MB
Use YARA to scan a sample directory and classify files, then analyze false positives to improve rule specificity
common_mistakes: Using single-byte or very short hex patterns that match legitimate binaries
Not testing rules against a corpus of known-good files to measure false positive rate
Including strings that are common across many different malware families (e.g., generic Windows API function names)

topics.title: Detection-as-Code (DaC) and CI/CD
concepts: Detection-as-Code treats detection rules as software artifacts: version controlled, tested, peer-reviewed, and deployed via CI/CD
Pipeline components: Git repository → CI testing (rule validation, false positive testing, unit tests) → deployment to SIEM (via API) → monitoring and feedback
Tools: Sigma rules as source, pySigma for validation, GitHub Actions/GitLab CI for pipeline, SIEM APIs for deployment
Rule lifecycle: development → review → testing (against attack and benign datasets) → deployment → tuning → retirement
Detection Engineering Maturity Model: ad-hoc → documented → versioned → automated → measured
key_facts: Every detection rule should have a defined lifecycle: creation, deployment, monitoring (performance metrics), tuning, and eventual retirement
CI/CD for detections should include: YAML linting, Sigma schema validation, false positive testing against known-good log samples, and true positive testing against known attack datasets
SOC Prime, splunk/security_content, and SigmaHQ provide rule repositories that can be consumed in DaC pipelines
Rule metrics to track: true positive rate, false positive rate, mean time to detect (MTTD), rule coverage across ATT&CK techniques

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers impair defenses (T1562) by disabling AV, EDR, or security logging. Detection-as-Code ensures the defender has version-controlled, tested, and rapidly deployable rules — so when a new evasion technique is discovered, a new detection can be pushed within hours instead of weeks.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: A mature DaC pipeline means the defender can iterate detection coverage quickly. An attacker who discovers a new bypass technique knows that once the technique is reported, the community will rapidly create and share Sigma/YARA rules. The attacker's window of opportunity shrinks with every rule deployed.
bypass_attempts: Developing novel techniques that no existing rule covers (zero-day evasion)
Rapidly rotating infrastructure and techniques to stay ahead of detection deployment
Targeting the DaC pipeline itself (compromising the Git repo or CI/CD to inject malicious rules)

drills: Set up a GitHub repository with Sigma rules, create a GitHub Actions workflow that validates rules using pySigma and deploys them to Splunk via the Splunk REST API on merge to main
Create a test dataset (attack logs + benign logs) and write automated tests that verify each Sigma rule fires on attack data but not on benign data
common_mistakes: Deploying rules without testing against benign traffic — leading to alert storms on first deployment
Not tracking rule performance metrics after deployment — stale rules with 99% false positive rates waste analyst time
Treating detection rules as 'set and forget' — rules decay as attacker techniques and legitimate tooling evolve

topics.title: Detection Tuning and False Positive Management
concepts: False positive sources: legitimate admin activity, vulnerability scanners, approved software updates, scheduled tasks, third-party security tools
Tuning techniques: adding exclusion filters (Sigma filter rules), creating allowlists of known-good behaviors, adjusting thresholds, time-based filters, user/asset-based context
Alert fatigue: high false positive rates cause analysts to ignore alerts, missing real threats — target <50% FP rate for Tier 1 alerts
Rule analytics: track FP rate per rule, review rules with FP rate >90%, create suppression/exclusion lists
Contextual enrichment: enriching alerts with asset criticality, user role, threat intelligence, and historical baseline to improve triage accuracy
key_facts: Industry SOC false positive rates range from 40-90% — reducing this is a top SOC priority
Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys) are a top source of false positives — their scanning activity mimics attack patterns
Each tuning change should be documented and version-controlled in the DaC pipeline
Sigma supports separate 'filter' rules that suppress known-good behaviors from triggering detection rules

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers deliberately generate noise (mass scanning, repeated failed logins, living-off-the-land commands) to blend their activity into the sea of alerts and false positives, hoping their real actions get lost in the noise.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: An attacker benefits directly from the defender's alert fatigue. If the SOC is overwhelmed with false positives, the attacker's real intrusion is just another alert in a queue of thousands. Well-tuned detections with low FP rates mean the attacker's actions stand out clearly.
bypass_attempts: Mimicking legitimate vulnerability scanner activity patterns
Using admin tools and procedures that match the organization's baseline
Timing attacks to coincide with known periods of high alert volume (e.g., patch Tuesday)

drills: Take a detection rule with a high false positive rate and create a Sigma filter rule that excludes known-good processes and users, then measure the improvement
Build a dashboard showing false positive rate per rule over time, with automated alerts when any rule's FP rate exceeds 90%
common_mistakes: Blanket-suppressing alerts without investigating the root cause — may suppress true positives hiding in the noise
Not documenting tuning decisions — when a new analyst joins, they don't understand why certain behaviors are allowlisted
Tuning based on gut feel instead of data — use metrics to drive tuning decisions

modules.title: Network Security Monitoring
modules.objective: Deploy and analyze network security monitoring tools (Zeek, Suricata, NetFlow) to detect malicious network traffic and C2 communication.

topics.title: Zeek (Bro) for Network Security Monitoring
concepts: Zeek is a powerful network analysis framework (formerly Bro) that performs deep protocol analysis and generates rich structured logs

Zeek generates 50+ log types: conn.log (connections), dns.log (DNS queries), http.log (HTTP requests), ssl.log (SSL/TLS handshakes), files.log (files extracted from traffic), x509.log (certificates), weird.log (protocol anomalies), notice.log (Zeek detections)
Zeek is a passive network monitor (not an IPS) — it observes and logs but does not block
Zeek script framework allows custom detection logic using the Zeek scripting language
Zeek can extract files from network traffic for malware analysis (files.log + file extraction framework)
key_facts: conn.log is the foundation — records every connection with UID, source/dest IP, ports, duration, bytes sent/received, protocol
dns.log captures every DNS query and response — critical for detecting DNS tunneling and C2 beaconing
http.log captures HTTP method, URI, user-agent, status codes — essential for detecting web-based attacks and C2
ssl.log captures the TLS SNI (Server Name Indication) — the domain the client is connecting to, even in encrypted traffic
Zeek 'notice' framework generates alerts for predefined suspicious patterns (e.g., SSL certificate validation failures)

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers establish C2 channels (T1071 Application Layer Protocol) using HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, or custom protocols — Zeek logs all of these. Attackers also exfiltrate data via DNS tunneling (T1048.003) — Zeek dns.log captures the anomalous query patterns.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker's C2 traffic flows through a Zeek-monitored network, every connection, DNS query, and TLS handshake is logged with rich metadata. Even if the payload is encrypted, the connection metadata (timing, frequency, destinations, SNI) reveals the C2 pattern. DNS-based exfiltration is particularly hard to hide because dns.log captures query length, frequency, and entropy — all anomalous for tunneling.
bypass_attempts: Using domain-fronting to hide the true C2 destination behind CDN domains
Mimicking legitimate web traffic patterns (human-like timing, standard user-agents, common domains)
Using DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) to hide DNS queries from Zeek's DNS monitoring
Piggybacking C2 data on existing legitimate connections

drills: Analyze conn.log to identify C2 beaconing: group connections by destination IP and calculate the time delta between connections — regular intervals (low jitter) indicate C2 beaconing
Analyze dns.log for DNS tunneling: look for long subdomain labels (>50 chars), high entropy, high frequency of queries to a single domain
common_mistakes: Only looking at conn.log and ignoring protocol-specific logs (dns.log, http.log, ssl.log)
Not correlating Zeek logs with endpoint data — network activity alone rarely tells the full story
Not tuning Zeek notice actions — default notice.log can generate excessive noise

topics.title: Suricata IDS/IPS — Rule-Based Network Detection
concepts: Suricata is a high-performance open-source IDS/IPS that can both detect (IDS mode) and block (IPS mode) malicious network traffic
Suricata rule syntax: action protocol source_ip source_port -> dest_ip dest_port (rule_options)
Rule actions: alert, drop (IPS), reject (IPS — drop + send RST/ICMP), pass
Rule options: msg, content (pattern matching), pcre (regex), flow (direction, state), ttl, dsize, threshold, tag, reference, classtype, sid (signature ID), rev (revision)
Rule sets: Emerging Threats (ET) Open and ET Pro rulesets, custom rules for organization-specific threats
Suricata also provides protocol analysis logging (eve.json JSON output format for SIEM integration)
key_facts: Suricata rule header: alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET $HTTP_PORTS (msg:"Suspicious HTTP"; content:"/malicious/path"; sid:1000001; rev:1;)
IPS mode requires inline deployment (bridge/transparent mode or TAP with active response) — IDS mode works with passive SPAN/mirror ports
content matching is case-sensitive by default — use nocase modifier for case-insensitive matching
flow:established,to_server filters for established connections going to the server — reduces false positives
Suricata's eve.json provides JSON-formatted output for easy SIEM integration (alerts, flow, dns, http, tls events)

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exploit public-facing applications (T1190) such as web servers, VPN gateways, or databases — Suricata rules detect known exploit signatures, shellcode, and malicious payloads in network traffic. Suricata in IPS mode can also block these attacks in real-time.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker attempts to exploit a service and Suricata is in IDS mode, the attack succeeds but generates an alert. In IPS mode, the malicious packet is dropped silently — the attacker may see a connection timeout but no explicit rejection. The attacker must then develop exploit code that doesn't match known signatures, or find a path that bypasses the IDS/IPS entirely.
bypass_attempts: Fragmenting or encoding attack payloads to avoid content-based rule matching
Using encrypted channels (TLS) that Suricata cannot inspect without TLS interception (MITM proxy)
Developing novel exploit variants that don't match existing signatures
Routing traffic through allowed protocols or paths that aren't inspected

drills: Write a Suricata rule to detect HTTP requests to a known C2 URL path: alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"Known C2 Communication"; content:"/gate.php"; http_uri; sid:20240001; rev:1;)
Deploy Suricata in IDS mode on a SPAN port and analyze the eve.json output in your SIEM for the top 10 alert signatures
common_mistakes: Not keeping ET rulesets updated — new rules are published daily for emerging threats
Running in IDS mode only when the organization actually needs IPS (blocking) capability
Not tuning rules — deploying the full ET ruleset generates thousands of alerts, most of which are noise for a specific environment

topics.title: NetFlow and Network Traffic Analysis
concepts: NetFlow (Cisco) / IPFIX / sFlow: network flow records summarizing traffic between source and destination (IP, port, protocol, bytes, packets, duration) without full packet content
Flow analysis for beaconing detection: regular intervals between connections to the same destination, low data volume per connection
Baselining: establishing normal traffic patterns (top destinations, typical data volumes, peak hours) to identify anomalies
NetFlow collection tools: nfdump/nfsen, flow-tools, ELK with logstash NetFlow input, commercial NDR platforms
Full packet capture (PCAP): tools like Arkime (formerly Moloch), n2disk, or tshark for deep-dive investigation of suspicious flows
key_facts: NetFlow provides connection metadata without payload — low storage cost, useful for long-term baselining
Beaconing (regular C2 check-ins) appears in NetFlow as connections to the same destination at regular intervals (e.g., every 60 seconds ± jitter)
Data exfiltration appears as high-volume, one-way traffic flows to unusual external destinations
Arkime (formerly Moloch) indexes PCAP for fast searching by IP, port, protocol, and payload strings
Network Detection and Response (NDR) platforms (ExtraHop, Darktrace, Vectra) use ML on flow data to detect anomalies

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exfiltrate stolen data over C2 channels (T1041) or use non-standard ports/protocols (T1571) to hide traffic. NetFlow captures the flow metadata — data volume, timing, destination — even when payload is encrypted.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: NetFlow analysis can detect the attacker's traffic patterns even when encryption hides the payload. A sudden spike in outbound data to a previously-unseen external IP, or connections to a specific destination every 45 seconds, are detectable anomalies. The attacker's challenge is that moving data out of the network inevitably generates traffic metadata that deviates from the baseline.
bypass_attempts: Exfiltrating data slowly over long periods ('low and slow') to avoid volume-based anomaly detection
Routing exfiltration through legitimate cloud services (AWS S3, Google Drive, Dropbox) that match normal traffic
Splitting data across multiple destinations and protocols to avoid correlation

drills: Use nfsen or Arkime to analyze NetFlow data — identify the top 10 destinations by total bytes transferred and flag any previously-unseen external destinations
Write a flow analysis query to detect beaconing: group connections by destination IP and calculate the standard deviation of inter-connection intervals
common_mistakes: Only looking at volume anomalies and missing low-and-slow exfiltration that doesn't spike
Not maintaining a baseline — without knowing normal traffic patterns, anomalies are impossible to identify
Ignoring internal-to-internal flows (east-west traffic) that may indicate lateral movement

topics.title: C2 Detection and Beaconing Analysis
concepts: Command and Control (C2) frameworks: Cobalt Strike (Malleable C2 profiles), Metasploit (Meterpreter), Sliver, Mythic, Brute Ratel — each has distinctive network behaviors
Beaconing characteristics: regular check-in intervals (typically 30-120 seconds), configurable jitter (±10-30%), small payload per check-in, HTTP/HTTPS/DNS/ICMP channels
Cobalt Strike Malleable C2 profiles: customize HTTP request/response structure, URI patterns, user-agent, headers, and data encoding to mimic legitimate traffic
Detection approaches: statistical beaconing analysis, JA3/JA3S TLS fingerprinting, HTTP header anomaly detection, domain age/reputation analysis
JA3 fingerprint: hash of TLS client hello parameters — identifies malware C2 clients even with valid certificates
key_facts: Cobalt Strike is the most common C2 framework used by both red teams and threat actors — its default beacon profiles are well-documented
JA3/JA3S TLS fingerprinting identifies C2 clients by their unique TLS handshake characteristics regardless of the domain or certificate used
Beacon detection requires analyzing connection timing over extended periods (hours to days) — a single connection reveals nothing
The DFIR Report provides excellent real-world analysis of Cobalt Strike intrusions and C2 detection
Malleable C2 profiles can be identified by analyzing HTTP GET/POST structure, URI patterns, and custom headers

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers establish C2 infrastructure using frameworks like Cobalt Strike with Malleable C2 profiles customized to mimic legitimate web traffic (T1071.001 Web Protocols). They may also use encrypted channels (T1573) to hide C2 communication.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker knows their C2 traffic is the lifeline of the operation. If C2 is detected and blocked, the entire foothold is lost. They invest heavily in making C2 traffic look legitimate — using real domains, valid TLS certificates, and traffic patterns that mimic browsing. But the statistical regularity of beaconing (even with jitter) and TLS fingerprint mismatches often betray them.
bypass_attempts: Customizing Malleable C2 profiles to perfectly mimic the organization's common web traffic
Using domain-fronting via legitimate CDN services (Azure, AWS, CloudFront) to hide the true C2 server
Increasing beacon interval and jitter to reduce statistical detectability
Using legitimate cloud services (Slack, Discord, Telegram, GitHub) as C2 channels

drills: Analyze Zeek conn.log or NetFlow data for beaconing patterns — sort connections by destination and calculate inter-connection time deltas; any destination with regular intervals is a beaconing candidate
Use JA3 fingerprinting (via Zeek SSL log or custom script) to identify all TLS clients with unusual fingerprints not matching known browsers
common_mistakes: Looking only at individual connections and missing the beaconing pattern that only emerges over time
Ignoring DNS-based C2 — DNS traffic is often trusted and not deeply inspected
Focusing only on outbound traffic and missing C2 over internal infrastructure (compromised internal servers as C2 relays)

topics.title: PCAP Analysis with Wireshark and tshark
concepts: Wireshark: GUI-based packet analyzer for deep inspection of network traffic (PCAP files)
Key Wireshark filters: ip.addr, tcp.port, http.request, tls.handshake, dns.qry.name, frame contains, tcp.stream
tshark: command-line version for automated PCAP analysis: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri
Stream reassembly: following TCP streams to reconstruct application-layer conversations
File extraction: extracting transferred files from PCAP using Wireshark 'Export Objects' or tshark
key_facts: Wireshark display filters use a different syntax than capture filters (BPF) — display: http.request.method == "POST", capture: tcp port 80
Following TCP streams (tcp.stream eq N) reconstructs the full application-layer conversation for investigation
TLS decryption requires the session keys (SSLKEYLOGFILE) — without keys, TLS traffic content is opaque
BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) capture filters are applied during capture to reduce PCAP size: 'host 10.0.0.1 and port 443'

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers communicate over the network using protocols that generate PCAP artifacts — HTTP requests, DNS queries, TLS handshakes. PCAP analysis allows deep inspection of the exact traffic, including payload patterns, timing, and protocol anomalies.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker's traffic is captured in a PCAP, every byte is preserved for forensic analysis. Even encrypted traffic reveals metadata (SNI, certificate details, timing, packet sizes). The attacker cannot control what the defender captures on the network — only what the payload contains (via encryption).
bypass_attempts: Using end-to-end encryption that prevents payload inspection even with TLS key capture
Piggybacking on legitimate, already-encrypted sessions where PCAP analysis only sees encrypted blobs
Minimizing network traffic to reduce the forensic footprint in PCAP captures

drills: Download a PCAP from Malware-Traffic-Analysis.net and use Wireshark to identify the C2 server, extract the malware payload, and document the attack chain
Use tshark to extract all HTTP POST requests from a PCAP and identify any with suspicious parameters
common_mistakes: Not using display filters effectively — scrolling through thousands of packets without filtering
Ignoring the 'Follow TCP Stream' feature for reconstructing full conversations
Not correlating PCAP findings with endpoint logs (Zeek logs, Sysmon events) for full context

modules.title: Security Operations Center (SOC) Operations
modules.objective: Operate within a SOC environment: triage alerts, escalate incidents, follow playbooks, and track performance metrics.

topics.title: SOC Structure, Tiers, and Roles
concepts: SOC tier structure: Tier 1 (alert triage, initial investigation, escalation), Tier 2 (deep investigation, threat hunting, tuning), Tier 3 (advanced forensics, IR, detection engineering)
SOC roles: SOC Analyst, Detection Engineer, Threat Hunter, Incident Responder, SOC Manager, Threat Intelligence Analyst
SOC models: in-house SOC, MSSP (Managed Security Service Provider), hybrid SOC, virtual SOC, SOC-as-a-Service (MDR)
SOC tools: SIEM, SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response), ticketing system (Jira, ServiceNow), threat intelligence platform, collaboration tools
Modern SOC evolution: AI-assisted triage, autonomous SOC, tier flattening (reducing handoff delays between tiers)
key_facts: Tier 1 analysts spend 60-80% of their time on alert triage — maximizing their efficiency is critical
SOCs should aim for a tier ratio of roughly 3:2:1 (Tier 1:Tier 2:Tier 3) to handle alert volume appropriately
MDR (Managed Detection and Response) and MSSP models are increasingly popular for organizations that cannot staff a 24/7 SOC
SOAR platforms automate repetitive triage steps, enrichment, and containment actions — reducing MTTD/MTTR

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers launch mass phishing campaigns (T1566) generating thousands of alerts that flood the SOC queue — hoping to overwhelm Tier 1 analysts and slip through as false negatives.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker exploits SOC alert fatigue as a defense bypass. A well-staffed, well-tooled SOC with efficient triage processes can investigate each alert thoroughly. A fatigued SOC with high MTTD gives the attacker more dwell time. The attacker's ideal scenario is blending into the noise of legitimate alerts.
bypass_attempts: Timing attacks during off-hours or weekends when SOC staffing is reduced
Generating decoy attacks to distract the SOC while the real attack proceeds on a different vector
Using slow, low-volume techniques that don't trigger individual alert thresholds

drills: Shadow or simulate Tier 1 triage: process 20 security alerts, classify each as true positive / false positive / needs investigation, and document your reasoning
Create a process flow diagram showing how an alert moves from detection → Tier 1 triage → Tier 2 investigation → escalation to IR
common_mistakes: Not documenting triage decisions — creating knowledge gaps when experienced analysts leave
Over-relying on escalation to higher tiers instead of developing Tier 1 capabilities
Not measuring SOC metrics (MTTD, MTTR, FP rate) — you cannot improve what you don't measure

topics.title: Alert Triage Workflow and Investigation
concepts: Triage process: receive alert → validate (is data complete?) → contextualize (enrich with asset, user, threat intel) → investigate (query SIEM) → classify (TP, FP, benign TP) → respond or escalate
Key triage questions: What happened? Is it still happening? What systems/users are affected? What is the asset criticality? Have we seen this before?
Enrichment sources: threat intelligence (IP/domain/hash known-malicious?), asset inventory, user context, historical correlation
Alert classification: True Positive (TP), False Positive (FP), Benign True Positive (BTP — real but legitimate activity)
Escalation criteria: confirmed malware execution, credential compromise, lateral movement, data exfiltration, or impact to critical assets
key_facts: Effective triage requires 3 data sources: the alert itself, endpoint context (what process/user triggered it), and network context (what connections occurred)
The most common triage mistake is closing an alert as 'false positive' without full investigation — always verify before closing
Benign True Positives (legitimate activity that triggers detection) should be documented and used to tune detections
Triage SLAs define maximum time-to-acknowledge and time-to-resolve for each severity (Critical: acknowledge <15min, resolve <4hr)

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers execute suspicious commands (T1059) that trigger alerts — the defender's triage process determines whether the alert is investigated promptly or buried in the queue. Attackers count on slow triage to extend their dwell time.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When an attacker triggers an alert, they are in a race against the SOC triage time. If the SOC has a 30-minute average triage time, the attacker has 30 minutes to achieve their objective or move laterally. Efficient triage directly reduces attacker dwell time.
bypass_attempts: Triggering numerous decoy alerts to delay triage of the real incident
Using techniques that generate ambiguous alerts (e.g., living off the land) that are harder to triage
Operating slowly to avoid triggering time-based alert thresholds

drills: Triage a simulated phishing alert: extract the URL/hash, check it against VirusTotal, determine if any user clicked, query SIEM for subsequent process executions
Build a triage checklist/playbook for a common alert type (e.g., 'unusual PowerShell execution') with step-by-step investigation questions
common_mistakes: Closing alerts based on the alert title alone without reading the full alert detail and supporting evidence
Not enriching alerts with asset criticality — treating a developer workstation alert the same as a Domain Controller alert
Inconsistent triage quality across analysts — no standardized process leads to some alerts being investigated properly and others being rubber-stamped

topics.title: Incident Response Playbooks and Runbooks
concepts: Playbook: a documented step-by-step procedure for responding to specific incident types (phishing, ransomware, credential compromise, web application attack)
Runbook: a more granular, technical set of instructions for executing a specific task within a playbook (e.g., 'block an IP in the firewall', 'isolate a host')
SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response): platforms like Splunk SOAR (Phantom), Palo Alto XSOAR, IBM Resilient, Swimlane that automate playbook execution
Key playbooks: Phishing Response, Ransomware Response, Credential Compromise, Insider Threat, Malware Infection, Data Exfiltration, DDoS, Business Email Compromise (BEC)
Playbook structure: trigger, triage steps, investigation steps, containment options, eradication steps, recovery steps, post-incident actions
key_facts: Playbooks standardize response — ensuring consistent quality regardless of which analyst handles the incident
SOAR automation can handle common playbook steps automatically: enriching alerts, containing threats, creating tickets
The most critical playbook is Ransomware Response — speed of containment directly impacts the number of systems encrypted
Playbooks should be living documents — updated after every incident based on lessons learned

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers deploy ransomware to encrypt data (T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact) — the ransomware playbook defines the rapid response: isolate affected hosts, identify patient zero, check for lateral movement, preserve evidence, assess backup integrity.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: Ransomware attackers operate on speed — the longer the defender takes to isolate affected systems, the more systems get encrypted. A well-executed ransomware playbook with automated host isolation (SOAR) can contain the blast radius in minutes instead of hours.
bypass_attempts: Deploying ransomware simultaneously across all systems (mass detonation) to overwhelm the response
Disabling or deleting backups before deploying ransomware (removing the recovery option)
Using living-off-the-land tools for lateral movement so containment playbooks targeting malware are ineffective

drills: Walk through the Phishing Response playbook: receive a phishing report → analyze the email → identify affected users → check for payload execution → contain → eradicate → document
Create a runbook for 'how to isolate a host from the network' covering both EDR-based isolation and manual switch port disable
common_mistakes: Playbooks that are too theoretical — analysts cannot execute steps that lack concrete, actionable instructions
Not testing playbooks via tabletop exercises — discovering during a real incident that the playbook is outdated
Automating too much via SOAR — automated containment actions can cause outages if not properly scoped

topics.title: SOC Metrics and KPIs
concepts: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect): average time from incident start to detection — industry target: <24 hours for high-severity incidents
MTTR (Mean Time to Respond/Resolve): average time from detection to containment/resolution — industry target: <4 hours for critical incidents
False Positive Rate (FPR): percentage of alerts that are not real threats — industry average: 40-90%; high-performing SOCs target <50%
Dwell Time: total time an attacker is in the environment undetected — industry average (Mandiant M-Trends): ~10-16 days
Coverage metrics: ATT&CK technique coverage (% of ATT&CK techniques with at least one detection rule)
Analyst metrics: alerts handled per shift, average time per alert, escalation accuracy
key_facts: Dwell time is the ultimate blue-team metric — Mandiant M-Trends reports global median dwell time of ~10 days
A 90%+ false positive rate means analysts are spending 90% of their time on noise — this is the #1 SOC efficiency problem
MTTD and MTTR should be tracked by severity — Critical incidents need much faster detection/response than Low
Map detection rules to ATT&CK techniques — identify techniques with no detection coverage and prioritize creating rules

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers use valid accounts (T1078) to operate undetected — every hour of undetected activity extends the attacker's dwell time and increases damage. The defender's MTTD directly measures how quickly they catch this.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: Dwell time is the attacker's key metric too — the longer they remain undetected, the more objectives they can accomplish. The attacker's goal is to maximize dwell time; the defender's goal is to minimize MTTD. Every SOC metric is ultimately about shrinking the attacker's window of opportunity.
bypass_attempts: Using legitimate credentials and tools to maximize dwell time without triggering detection thresholds
Moving slowly and deliberately to avoid creating anomalous patterns
Cleaning up artifacts to prevent retrospective detection

drills: Calculate MTTD and MTTR from a set of 10 simulated incidents — identify which incident types have the longest detection/response times
Map your detection rules to MITRE ATT&CK techniques and identify the top 5 techniques with no detection coverage
common_mistakes: Measuring only volume metrics (alerts per day) without quality metrics (FP rate, TP rate)
Not benchmarking against industry standards (Mandiant M-Trends, Verizon DBIR) for context
Vanity metrics — tracking metrics that look good but don't drive improvement

modules.title: Incident Response — Frameworks and Execution
modules.objective: Execute the full incident response lifecycle using NIST SP 800-61 and SANS PICERL frameworks, from preparation through lessons learned.

topics.title: NIST SP 800-61 Incident Response Lifecycle
concepts: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 defines a 4-phase lifecycle: (1) Preparation, (2) Detection & Analysis, (3) Containment, Eradication & Recovery, (4) Post-Incident Activity
NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 adds 'Coordination' as a cross-cutting activity — emphasizing communication with stakeholders, leadership, legal, and external parties
Preparation phase: IR plan, contact lists, toolkits (forensic, analysis), jump bags, training, tabletop exercises, communication plan
Detection & Analysis: alert triage, log analysis, scope determination, severity classification
Containment: short-term (isolate affected hosts) and long-term (remediate root cause) containment strategies
Eradication: remove malware, close vulnerability, rebuild compromised systems
Recovery: restore from backup, validate system integrity, monitor for reinfection
Post-Incident Activity: lessons learned, report writing, process improvement, evidence retention
key_facts: NIST SP 800-61r2 is the foundational US government incident response guidance, published in 2012
NIST SP 800-61r3 (2024) modernizes the guidance to include cloud incidents, supply chain attacks, and coordination frameworks
Incident severity levels: Low (limited impact), Medium (significant impact to non-critical systems), High (critical system compromise), Emergency (organization-wide threat)
The Preparation phase is the most important — 80% of IR effectiveness comes from preparation done before an incident occurs
Post-incident review (lessons learned) should be blameless — focused on process improvement, not individual fault

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers execute the full kill chain culminating in impact (T1486 ransomware) — the defender's IR lifecycle determines how quickly they can contain, eradicate, and recover.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker knows that their success depends on the defender's chaos. If the defender has no IR plan, unclear roles, and no tested procedures, the attacker has maximum time to operate. If the defender has a mature IR program (tested plans, clear roles, automated containment), the attacker's window is dramatically shorter.
bypass_attempts: Deploying ransomware rapidly to minimize the defender's containment window
Disrupting communication channels to delay coordination during the incident
Targeting backup systems to impair the Recovery phase

drills: Map a real-world incident (from The DFIR Report) to the NIST 800-61 phases — document what happened in each phase and identify where the response could have been faster
Review your organization's IR plan and identify gaps: missing contact lists, no tested containment procedures, no defined severity classification
common_mistakes: Treating IR as a reactive activity — not investing in the Preparation phase
Skipping Post-Incident Activity because teams are exhausted — the lessons learned phase is what improves future responses
Blame-focused post-incident reviews — cause analysts to hide mistakes instead of sharing them

topics.title: SANS PICERL Framework
concepts: SANS PICERL is a 6-phase incident response framework: (P)reparation, (I)dentification, (C)ontainment, (E)radication, (R)ecovery, (L)essons Learned
Preparation: policies, procedures, training, tools, communication channels, IR team roles
Identification: detecting the incident, determining scope, classifying severity, activating the IR team
Containment: isolating affected systems, stopping the spread — short-term (immediate isolation) and long-term (sustained containment with remediation)
Eradication: removing the threat — malware removal, vulnerability patching, account resets, credential rotation
Recovery: restoring systems to normal operation — from backup, rebuilt systems, monitoring for reinfection
Lessons Learned: post-incident review, report, improvement actions, updating IR plans and detections
key_facts: PICERL is the SANS Institute's IR framework — widely used in industry and taught in SANS SEC504
The 'C' (Containment) is often the most critical and time-sensitive phase — especially for ransomware
Lessons Learned should be scheduled within 1-2 weeks of incident closure while details are fresh — use a blameless format
Containment decisions should be documented and pre-authorized — during an incident, you don't want to wait for approval to isolate a compromised host
PICERL maps directly to NIST 800-61 phases — the frameworks are complementary, not competing

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers move laterally using remote services like SMB, RDP, WinRM (T1021) — each new system they reach expands the containment scope. The defender's Containment phase must cut off all attacker access points, not just the initial compromise.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's lateral movement directly complicates the defender's Containment phase. Each new system the attacker compromises is another system the defender must identify, isolate, and clean. The attacker's strategy is to maximize lateral spread before the defender enters the Containment phase.
bypass_attempts: Rapidly spreading to many systems before the defender begins containment
Using legitimate credentials so containment requires account disabling (disrupting business)
Establishing multiple independent persistence mechanisms so eradication is incomplete

drills: Run a tabletop exercise using PICERL: given a ransomware scenario, walk through each phase and document actions, responsible parties, and tools needed
Create a Lessons Learned template: incident summary, timeline, what went well, what went wrong, root cause analysis, action items with owners
common_mistakes: Rushing to Eradication before Containment is complete — removing malware while the attacker still has access leads to reinfection
Not conducting Lessons Learned sessions — repeating the same mistakes on the next incident
Inadequate scoping during Identification — missing compromised systems during containment leads to recurring incidents

topics.title: Containment and Eradication Strategies
concepts: Containment methods: host isolation (EDR network isolation, switch port disable, firewall rules), account suspension, credential reset, firewall blocking (IP, domain, port), email quarantine, DNS sinkholing
Short-term containment: immediate actions to stop the bleeding (isolate the infected host, block the C2 IP)
Long-term containment: sustained measures while eradication is planned (segmented VLAN, monitoring-only mode, temporary firewall rules)
Eradication: malware removal, vulnerability patching, removing persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, services, registry Run keys, WMI subscriptions), rebuilding from known-good images
Decision factors for containment: business impact of isolating the system, risk of lateral movement, evidence preservation needs
key_facts: EDR-based host isolation is the fastest containment method — network-isolating a host via EDR takes seconds vs. minutes for manual switch port disable
Always preserve forensic evidence (memory dump, disk image) BEFORE eradicating — once the system is rebuilt, artifacts are lost
Credential rotation is mandatory during eradication — the attacker likely has credentials; if you don't reset them, they will regain access
Rebuilding from a known-good image is the gold standard for eradication — cleaning an infected system is risky
Containment scope must cover ALL compromised systems — missing one leads to reinfection (the most common cause of incident recurrence)

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers establish persistence using multiple mechanisms (T1547 Boot/Logon Autostart Execution, T1136 Create Account) — eradication must find and remove ALL persistence mechanisms or the attacker returns.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's persistence mechanisms are their insurance policy. If the defender removes one mechanism but misses another (e.g., removes the malicious service but misses the WMI subscription), the attacker can regain access. The attacker deliberately creates multiple independent persistence paths to survive eradication.
bypass_attempts: Creating multiple independent persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, services, registry, WMI, COM objects)
Using credential-based persistence (creating new admin accounts) that survives system rebuilds if AD wasn't cleaned
Establishing persistence in infrastructure the defender might not check (network devices, IoT, cloud)

drills: Create a containment decision tree: 'if system is a Domain Controller → do NOT isolate, use monitoring + credential reset; if workstation → EDR isolate immediately'

List all common Windows persistence locations and create a forensic checklist for eradication: Run/RunOnce keys, Services, Scheduled Tasks, WMI Event Subscriptions, COM hijacking, AppInit_DLLs, Startup folder
common_mistakes: Not preserving forensic evidence before eradication — destroying the crime scene makes post-incident analysis impossible
Partial eradication — missing persistence mechanisms leads to incident recurrence within days
Not rotating credentials — the attacker returns with stolen credentials even after all malware is removed

topics.title: Tabletop Exercises and Purple Teaming
concepts: Tabletop exercise (TTX): a discussion-based simulation where the IR team walks through an incident scenario — no actual systems are affected, focus is on process and decision-making
TTX formats: facilitator-led scenario walkthrough, inject-based (new information introduced during the exercise), functional (some technical execution on isolated systems)
TTX participants: IR team, IT operations, legal, HR, communications/PR, executive leadership, third-party responders
CISA Tabletop Exercise Packages (CTEPs): free pre-built scenarios (ransomware, data breach, supply chain) for organizations
Purple teaming: red team executes attacks while blue team detects and responds — live collaboration to improve both offense and defense
key_facts: Tabletop exercises should be conducted at least annually, and after any major organizational or infrastructure change
CISA provides free tabletop exercise packages at cisa.gov — covering ransomware, data breaches, and supply chain attacks
Purple team exercises are the most effective way to validate detection coverage — you confirm whether your rules actually fire against real attacks
TTX objectives should be specific and measurable: 'validate the ransomware communication plan', 'test the external IR retainer activation'
After-action report (AAR): document what went well, what didn't, and specific improvement actions with owners and deadlines

offense_pairing.what_red_does: In a purple team exercise, the red team executes the full attack chain (phishing → credential theft → lateral movement → ransomware) and the blue team attempts to detect and respond at each stage. Gaps are identified and remediated.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: From the attacker's perspective, a well-exercised SOC is a hardened target. Each purple team exercise closes detection gaps and tightens response procedures. The attacker doesn't know which techniques will be detected, making each operation riskier. In contrast, a SOC that never exercises will be slow, confused, and error-prone during a real incident.
bypass_attempts: Using novel techniques not covered in previous exercises — the SOC may not have detections for them
Exploiting gaps between exercises — techniques validated 6 months ago may have degraded if rules haven't been maintained
Targeting the exercise process itself — timing attacks to coincide with known exercise schedules

drills: Facilitate a ransomware tabletop exercise using a CISA CTEP package — walk through scenario injects, document team decisions, produce an after-action report

Conduct a mini purple team exercise: red team simulates a phishing-to-ransomware chain using Atomic Red Team, blue team monitors SIEM — identify which ATT&CK techniques were detected and which were missed
common_mistakes: Tabletop exercises that are too easy — scenarios should be challenging enough to expose real gaps
Not involving business stakeholders (legal, PR, leadership) — during a real incident, these groups are critical
Not following up on after-action report action items — the exercise is wasted if improvement actions aren't completed

modules.title: Threat Hunting Methodologies
modules.objective: Design and execute structured threat hunts using hypothesis-driven and TTP-based methodologies, mapping findings to MITRE ATT&CK.

topics.title: Hypothesis-Driven Threat Hunting
concepts: Threat hunting is the proactive, human-driven search for threats that have evaded existing detection capabilities — unlike alert-driven response, hunting assumes the attacker is already in the environment
Hypothesis structure: 'If [attacker technique] is present, then we should observe [observable artifact] in [data source]'
Hypothesis sources: MITRE ATT&CK techniques, threat intelligence reports, emerging vulnerabilities/CVEs, lessons from previous incidents, known gaps in detection coverage
SQRRL / MITRE TTP-Based Hunting methodology: select ATT&CK technique → identify relevant data sources → formulate hypothesis → collect and analyze data → validate findings → create new detections
PEAK Framework (Splunk): Prepare, Execute, Analyze, Knowledge — structured hunting lifecycle with hypothesis, analytics, and knowledge output
key_facts: The Splunk PEAK framework defines hypothesis types: situational (based on current threat), environmental (based on environment analysis), and hypothetical (based on attack theory)
Hypotheses should be specific, testable, and falsifiable — 'look for bad stuff' is not a hypothesis
Every successful hunt should result in a new detection rule — converting manual hunting into automated detection
MITRE's TTP-Based Hunting paper (2019) is the foundational document for structured, ATT&CK-driven hunting
Threat hunting maturity model (SQRRL): HM1 (automated alert analysis), HM2 (structured investigation), HM3 (intelligence-driven hunting), HM4 (custom hunting with data science)

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers dump credentials (T1003) using techniques that may not trigger existing alerts — the threat hunter proactively searches for evidence of credential dumping activity regardless of whether alerts fired.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The threat hunter is the attacker's worst enemy in the SOC — unlike alert-driven analysts who respond to known-bad patterns, hunters proactively look for anomalies that may indicate novel attack techniques. An attacker who evaded all alerts can still be caught by a hunter who notices the behavioral footprint: unusual process relationships, anomalous network connections, or out-of-baseline data access patterns.
bypass_attempts: Minimizing footprint — executing only necessary actions, cleaning up artifacts
Blending with legitimate admin activity — using the same tools and procedures as real administrators
Operating slowly over extended periods to make patterns less noticeable in time-bounded hunt queries

drills: Formulate a hunting hypothesis for T1003.001 (LSASS Memory access): 'If an attacker dumped LSASS memory, then we should observe a process accessing lsass.exe with granted access rights including PROCESS_VM_READ in Sysmon Event ID 10 logs' — execute the hunt in your SIEM
Using the PEAK framework, design a hunt for detecting lateral movement via PsExec: identify data sources, formulate the hypothesis, execute the query, document findings
common_mistakes: Hunting without a hypothesis — aimless log searching wastes time and rarely produces actionable results
Not converting successful hunts into automated detections — the same manual hunt needs to be repeated if not automated
Only hunting for known techniques — the most valuable hunts target novel or emerging techniques that existing detections don't cover

topics.title: TTP-Based Hunting with MITRE ATT&CK
concepts: TTP (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) hunting focuses on attacker behaviors rather than specific indicators (IPs, hashes, domains) — TTPs are harder for attackers to change
ATT&CK-based hunt workflow: identify target technique → identify relevant data sources → understand expected normal behavior → identify anomalies → investigate → create detection
Pyramid of Pain (David Bianco): hash values (trivial to change) → IP addresses → domain names → host artifacts → network artifacts → TTPs (most painful for attacker to change)
ATT&CK Navigator: visualize technique coverage and gaps — map detection coverage to the ATT&CK matrix to identify hunting priorities
Threat group profiles: MITRE ATT&CK documents TTPs used by specific threat groups (APT29, FIN7, etc.) — hunt for group-specific techniques when relevant intelligence is available
key_facts: The Pyramid of Pain concept: detecting TTPs causes the most 'pain' to attackers because changing tactics and techniques requires fundamental retooling
TTPs at the top of the pyramid persist across campaigns, infrastructure changes, and tool updates — making them the highest-value detection targets
ATT&CK Navigator provides a visual heatmap of detection coverage — red cells = no detection, green cells = covered
Atomic Red Team (Red Canary) provides small, portable tests for each ATT&CK technique — useful for validating hunts
Mapping hunts to ATT&CK techniques enables systematic coverage analysis — 'we have hunts for 45% of ATT&CK Enterprise techniques'

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers use TTPs like process injection (T1055) and persistence mechanisms (T1547) that are fundamental to their methodology. TTP-based hunting searches for the behavioral patterns of these techniques regardless of the specific tools or malware used.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When the defender hunts at the TTP level, the attacker faces the Pyramid of Pain — to evade TTP-based detection, they must change their fundamental techniques, not just rotate infrastructure or recompile malware. A defender hunting for 'process injection behavior' forces the attacker to abandon process injection entirely, not just rename their injector tool.
bypass_attempts: Developing entirely new techniques not covered by existing TTP detections (the most expensive option)
Using techniques so common in the environment that they're hard to distinguish from normal activity
Operating at a layer not monitored by the TTP hunt (e.g., kernel-mode operations if the hunt only looks at user-mode activity)

drills: Select 3 ATT&CK techniques with no detection coverage (use ATT&CK Navigator to identify gaps) — design and execute a TTP-based hunt for each, then create Sigma rules for confirmed detections
Use Atomic Red Team to simulate T1055.001 (Process Injection via DLL injection) and verify your hunting query detects the activity
common_mistakes: Hunting for indicators (IPs, hashes) instead of TTPs — indicators are cheap for attackers to change
Not validating hunt results — a hunt query with 1000 results is useless without investigation to find the true positives
Ignoring false positive rate when converting hunts to detections — a hunt with 90% FP rate is not deployable as an automated detection

topics.title: Hunting for Living Off the Land (LOTL) Activity
concepts: Living Off the Land (LOTL): attackers use legitimate, built-in OS tools (LOLBins/LOLScripts) to accomplish objectives without deploying custom malware

Common LOLBins: certutil.exe (file download, base64 decode), bitsadmin.exe (file download), regsvr32.exe (remote script execution), mshta.exe (HTA execution), wmic.exe (remote process execution), rundll32.exe, PowerShell, cmd.exe
The LOLBAS Project (lolbas-project.github.io) catalogs all known living-off-the-land binaries and scripts
Detection strategy: baseline legitimate usage patterns and detect anomalies — unusual execution context, unexpected parent processes, suspicious command-line arguments
PowerShell detection: Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) captures the full script content even if obfuscated — AMSI integration provides de-obfuscated content
key_facts: PowerShell appears in ~71% of documented LOTL attack cases (Vectra AI telemetry)
LOTL attacks appear in ~84% of high-severity breaches — they are the dominant attack technique because they bypass signature-based detection
certutil.exe with -urlcache or -decode flags is a strong indicator of file download or decoding by an attacker
Event ID 4104 (PowerShell Script Block Logging) captures the de-obfuscated script — even if the attacker uses -enc (base64 encoded), the logged scriptblock contains cleartext
AMSI (Anti-Malware Scan Interface) integrates with PowerShell to scan script content before execution

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers abuse LOLBins (T1218 System Binary Proxy Execution, T1059.001 PowerShell) to execute code using trusted, signed system tools that are whitelisted and blend with normal administrative activity.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's advantage with LOTL is that they use tools already present, signed by the OS vendor, and typically whitelisted. The defender cannot simply block certutil.exe or PowerShell without breaking legitimate admin workflows. The attacker's challenge is that behavioral baselining can still detect anomalous usage.
bypass_attempts: Using LOLBins in ways that match the organization's legitimate admin patterns (requires recon)
Combining multiple LOLBins in chains that individually look benign but collectively accomplish malicious objectives
Using lesser-known LOLBins not yet on the defender's monitoring list

drills: Hunt for suspicious certutil usage: search for certutil.exe with arguments -urlcache, -decode, -encode, or -split in Sysmon EID 1 or PowerShell logs
Hunt for LOLBin execution from unexpected directories: Sysmon EID 1 where Image matches *\Temp\* or *\AppData\*
common_mistakes: Blocking LOLBins entirely — this breaks legitimate admin workflows
Only looking for known-bad command-line patterns — attackers use encoding, aliases, and combinations to evade string matching
Not establishing baselines — without knowing how PowerShell and other LOLBins are legitimately used, you cannot identify anomalies

topics.title: Hunting for Persistence Mechanisms
concepts: Common Windows persistence locations: Registry Run/RunOnce keys, Scheduled Tasks, Services, WMI Event Subscriptions, COM Object hijacking, AppInit_DLLs, Winlogon Shell, Startup folder, BITS jobs
Sysmon persistence detection: EID 12 (Registry add/delete), EID 13 (Registry value set), EID 11 (File creation) — configure to monitor persistence-relevant registry keys
Autoruns (Sysinternals): comprehensive tool for enumerating all auto-start extension points (ASEPs)
Persistence hunting methodology: enumerate all persistence points → baseline → compare against known-good → investigate new/modified entries
ATT&CK persistence techniques: T1547 (Boot/Logon Autostart), T1053 (Scheduled Task/Job), T1543 (Create/Modify System Process), T1136 (Create Account), T1098 (Account Manipulation)
key_facts: Registry Run Keys (T1547.001) are the most common persistence mechanism — both HKLM (system-wide) and HKCU (user-specific)
WMI Event Subscriptions (T1546.003) are stealthy persistence — event filters, consumers, and bindings that execute code on system events
COM Object hijacking (T1546.015) is difficult to detect — attacker modifies HKCU registry for COM objects that legitimate applications use
Autoruns by Sysinternals is the gold-standard tool for enumerating persistence — autorunsc.exe outputs to CSV for SIEM ingestion
Scheduled tasks created by non-admin users or running unexpected executables are high-signal persistence indicators

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers establish persistence to survive reboots, credential changes, and initial cleanup — using registry Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, WMI subscriptions, and COM hijacking.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: Persistence is the attacker's anchor in the environment — without it, a reboot or cleanup evicts them. But every persistence mechanism creates detectable artifacts: registry entries, scheduled task definitions, service configurations, file drops. The attacker must choose between well-known persistence locations (likely monitored) and obscure ones (harder to create, harder to maintain).
bypass_attempts: Using stealthy persistence mechanisms (WMI subscriptions, COM hijacking) that don't appear in standard autoruns scans
Piggybacking on existing legitimate scheduled tasks or services
Using credential-based persistence instead of system-based — creating new admin accounts

drills: Run Autoruns (autorunsc.exe) on a lab system before and after executing Atomic Red Team persistence technique (e.g., T1547.001) — diff the outputs
Write a hunting query for WMI Event Subscriptions: query Sysmon EID 19/20/21 or use PowerShell Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventFilter
common_mistakes: Only checking common persistence locations (Run keys, Startup folder) and missing stealthy ones (WMI, COM hijacking)
Not baselining — without a known-good baseline, every persistence entry looks suspicious
Not understanding the legitimate persistence in the environment — many enterprise management tools deploy persistence that looks malicious

modules.title: Digital Forensics and DFIR
modules.objective: Conduct digital forensic investigations across disk, memory, and network evidence to reconstruct attacker activity and support incident response.

topics.title: Memory Forensics with Volatility
