concepts: Memory forensics: analysis of volatile RAM captures to find running malware, injected code, network connections, credentials, and process activity that may not exist on disk
Volatility 3 (current) / Volatility 2 (legacy): open-source memory forensics framework from the Volatility Foundation

Key Volatility 3 plugins: windows.pslist (process list via doubly-linked list), windows.psscan (scan for hidden/unlinked processes), windows.malfind (detect injected code via VAD tags + page permissions), windows.netscan (network connections), windows.dlllist (loaded DLLs per process), windows.cmdline (process command lines), windows.modscan (kernel modules)
Process injection indicators: malfind detects code with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE permissions in processes that shouldn't have executable memory regions
Memory acquisition tools: WinPMEM, DumpIt, LiME (Linux), Magnet RAM Capture
key_facts: pslist uses the active process list (doubly-linked list in EPROCESS); psscan scans memory for EPROCESS structures — psscan can find 'hidden' processes that DKOM removed from the active list
malfind is the primary tool for detecting code injection — it identifies memory regions with RWX permissions and MZ/PE headers that don't correspond to loaded DLLs
Volatility can extract credentials from memory — finding cleartext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets stored in LSASS process memory
Memory captures should be taken BEFORE shutting down the system — RAM is volatile and lost on power-off
Volatility 3 is Python 3-based with a plugin framework; Volatility 2 is Python 2 (end-of-life) but still used

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers inject malicious code into legitimate process memory (T1055 Process Injection) to hide from disk-based forensic analysis. They may also keep tools entirely in memory (fileless malware) without writing to disk.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's assumption is often that 'if it's not on disk, it can't be found.' Memory forensics shatters this assumption — injected code, hidden processes, network connections, and even decrypted credentials all live in RAM. An attacker who knows the defender will capture RAM must avoid injecting into processes and storing credentials in LSASS.
bypass_attempts: Using kernel-mode rootkits that manipulate memory structures to hide from Volatility plugins
Minimizing memory footprint — executing, then cleaning up injected code before a memory capture can be taken
Detecting memory acquisition tools and taking evasive action before capture completes

drills: Download a practice memory image (from Volatility Foundation samples) and run: vol.py -f memory.img windows.pslist, then windows.malfind, then windows.netscan — identify suspicious processes, injected code, and network connections
Use Volatility to extract credentials from a memory image containing an LSASS process
common_mistakes: Only running pslist and not psscan — missing hidden processes that rootkits unlink from the active process list
Not correlating memory forensics findings with disk forensics and network logs
Capturing memory too late — if the attacker has already cleaned up or rebooted, critical evidence is lost

topics.title: Disk Forensics with Autopsy and Sleuth Kit
concepts: Disk forensics: analysis of disk images (DD/E01) to recover files, examine file system artifacts, reconstruct timelines, and identify malware
Autopsy: GUI-based forensic platform built on The Sleuth Kit (TSK) — provides file analysis, keyword search, timeline, hash set matching
The Sleuth Kit (TSK): command-line forensic tools — fls (list files), icat (extract file by inode), mmls (partition table), tsk_recover (recover deleted files)

Key forensic artifacts: Prefetch files (.pf), Windows Registry hives (SAM, SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SECURITY, NTUSER.DAT), Event Logs (.evtx), ShimCache/AmCache (program execution history), browser history, LNK files, Jump Lists, $MFT, USN Journal
Timeline analysis: create a super timeline (using log2timeline/plaso) combining all artifact timestamps chronologically
key_facts: Prefetch files (.pf) in C:\Windows\Prefetch record every executable run on the system — excellent for proving malware execution
ShimCache (AppCompatCache) in the SYSTEM registry hive records application execution history — even for deleted executables
AmCache.hve records detailed metadata about executed programs including SHA-1 hashes, file paths, and execution timestamps
LNK files and Jump Lists record recently opened files and applications — can reveal files the attacker accessed
Plaso/log2timeline is the standard tool for creating forensic super-timelines — parses dozens of artifact types

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers attempt to cover their tracks (T1070 Indicator Removal) by deleting logs, clearing event logs, removing tools, and deleting prefetch files. Disk forensics recovers evidence from forensic artifacts that the attacker may not know about or cannot easily delete.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker faces an asymmetric battle on disk forensics: the Windows operating system records hundreds of forensic artifacts that are difficult to comprehensively delete. The attacker may clear Event Logs (generating Event 1102), delete their malware binary, and clean Prefetch — but ShimCache, AmCache, USN Journal, $MFT, and registry traces may still contain evidence. Complete cleanup is nearly impossible.
bypass_attempts: Comprehensive anti-forensics: deleting Prefetch, clearing ShimCache/AmCache, wiping $MFT entries, timestomping files
Using fileless malware that minimizes disk artifacts — operating entirely in memory
Disabling forensic artifact collection (e.g., disabling Prefetch via registry)

drills: Analyze a Windows disk image with Autopsy: examine Prefetch files, ShimCache, AmCache, and Event Logs to reconstruct what programs were executed and when
Use plaso (log2timeline) to create a super-timeline from a disk image and identify the time window of attacker activity
common_mistakes: Not examining Windows forensic artifacts beyond Event Logs — ShimCache, AmCache, Prefetch, and LNK files are critical
Only looking at allocated files and not examining unallocated space, slack space, and deleted file remnants
Not creating a timeline — individual artifacts are less useful than understanding the sequence of events

topics.title: Network Forensics and Evidence Collection
concepts: Network forensics: analysis of captured network traffic (PCAP) and network metadata (Zeek logs, NetFlow, firewall logs) to reconstruct attacker network activity
Full packet capture (PCAP): preserves the complete content of network traffic — essential for deep-dive analysis but storage-intensive
Network metadata (Zeek logs, NetFlow): lightweight summary of network activity — enables long-term retention and faster searching

Key analysis techniques: packet inspection (Wireshark/tshark), flow analysis (Zeek conn.log), DNS analysis (Zeek dns.log, passive DNS), TLS analysis (JA3/JA3S fingerprints, certificate analysis), file extraction
Network evidence sources: SPAN/mirror ports, network TAPs, IDS/IPS logs, firewall logs, proxy logs, DNS resolver logs
key_facts: Zeek logs are the primary network forensic evidence source in well-instrumented environments
Network forensics is critical for answering 'what data did the attacker exfiltrate?' — only network captures can show the actual data that left the environment
Passive DNS (pDNS) databases (Farsight DNSDB, VirusTotal) allow historical lookups of DNS associations
TLS interception (SSL decryption proxy) is required to inspect encrypted traffic content
Tools for large-scale PCAP analysis: Arkime (formerly Moloch) for indexed PCAP search

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exfiltrate data over the network (T1041 Exfil Over C2 Channel, T1048 Exfil Over Alternative Protocol) — network forensics captures the actual exfiltration events, including data volume, timing, destination, and sometimes the payload content.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: Network exfiltration is the attacker's most vulnerable moment — moving stolen data out of the environment inevitably creates network traffic that can be captured, analyzed, and attributed. The attacker must choose between: speed (large, obvious transfers), stealth (slow, small transfers), and protocol choice.
bypass_attempts: Exfiltrating via legitimate cloud services (AWS S3, Google Drive, Dropbox) that match normal business traffic patterns
Using DNS tunneling — encoding data in DNS queries which is often not deeply inspected
Exfiltrating data in small chunks over extended periods ('low and slow')
Encrypting exfiltrated data before transmission to prevent content inspection

drills: Analyze Zeek conn.log and dns.log from a known intrusion (from The DFIR Report or Malware-Traffic-Analysis.net): identify the C2 server, exfiltration volume, and timeline
Use Wireshark to extract a file transferred over HTTP from a PCAP: File → Export Objects → HTTP, then analyze the extracted file
common_mistakes: Not correlating network forensics with endpoint and disk forensics — each tells part of the story
Not retaining PCAP long enough — if PCAP is purged after 24 hours, retrospective investigation of older incidents is impossible
Ignoring east-west (internal) traffic — lateral movement generates network artifacts that are often missed

topics.title: DFIR Collection: KAPE, Velociraptor, and Eric Zimmerman Tools
concepts: KAPE (Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor): rapid forensic artifact collection tool — collects specific files/registry/artifacts from live or dead systems in minutes
KAPE modules: Targets (what to collect) and Modules (how to process — runs tools like RECmd, MFTECmd on collected data)
Velociraptor (Rapid7): open-source endpoint visibility, DFIR, and monitoring platform — uses VQL (Velociraptor Query Language) for forensic artifact collection at scale
Velociraptor VQL: SQL-like query language for endpoint data collection — can hunt across thousands of endpoints simultaneously
Eric Zimmerman tools: EZViewer (Registry viewer), RECmd (Registry batch processing), MFTECmd ($MFT parsing), LECmd (LNK file parsing), SBECmd (ShellBags parsing), PECmd (Prefetch parsing)
key_facts: KAPE can collect the most critical forensic artifacts (Event Logs, Registry hives, Prefetch, AmCache) from a Windows system in under 5 minutes
Velociraptor deploys lightweight agents to endpoints and enables centralized hunting — ideal for large-scale DFIR
Eric Zimmerman's tools are free and widely considered essential for Windows DFIR
The order of volatility (RFC 3227) guides evidence collection: CPU/registers → RAM → network state → running processes → disk → remote logs
KAPE and Velociraptor can be used together: Velociraptor deploys KAPE across endpoints for targeted artifact collection

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers establish persistence using registry keys, scheduled tasks, and services that leave forensic artifacts on disk. KAPE and Velociraptor enable rapid, targeted collection of these artifacts across hundreds of systems to identify every persistence mechanism deployed.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's persistence mechanisms are documented in forensic artifacts that KAPE and Velociraptor can rapidly collect and parse. Even if the attacker deletes the original malware, the forensic breadcrumbs (Prefetch showing execution, Registry showing persistence, AmCache showing file hashes) persist. At scale, the defender can check every endpoint for the same indicators in minutes.
bypass_attempts: Using persistence mechanisms that don't create common forensic artifacts (e.g., WMI subscriptions instead of Registry Run keys)
Cleaning up forensic artifacts (deleting Prefetch, clearing AmCache) after establishing persistence
Using fileless persistence that exists only in memory or registry values

drills: Deploy Velociraptor on a lab network and create a VQL hunt that searches all endpoints for suspicious Run keys in the registry
Use KAPE to triage-collect forensic artifacts from a compromised system: collect Event Logs, Registry hives, Prefetch, and AmCache, then process with Eric Zimmerman tools
common_mistakes: Collecting a full disk image when targeted artifact collection (KAPE) would be faster and more actionable
Not processing collected artifacts — collecting data is only half the job; parsing and analysis is essential
Not collecting evidence in order of volatility — if you image disk before capturing RAM, you lose volatile evidence

modules.title: Vulnerability Management and System Hardening
modules.objective: Run vulnerability scans, prioritize remediation using CVSS and threat context, and apply CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs to harden systems.

topics.title: Vulnerability Scanning with Nessus, OpenVAS, and Qualys
concepts: Vulnerability scanning: automated identification of known vulnerabilities (CVEs), misconfigurations, and missing patches across network assets
Nessus (Tenable): industry-standard vulnerability scanner — credentialed and non-credentialed scans, compliance audits
OpenVAS / Greenbone: open-source vulnerability scanner — alternative to Nessus
Qualys VMDR: cloud-based vulnerability management platform — includes discovery, assessment, prioritization, and patching
Scan types: discovery scans, vulnerability scans, compliance scans, authenticated scans
NVD (National Vulnerability Database): US government repository of vulnerability data, including CVSS scores
key_facts: Authenticated (credentialed) scans find significantly more vulnerabilities than unauthenticated scans
CVSS v3.1 scores range from 0-10: Low (0.1-3.9), Medium (4.0-6.9), High (7.0-8.9), Critical (9.0-10.0)
EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) from FIRST provides probability of exploitation within 30 days
CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) Catalog: vulnerabilities known to be actively exploited — should be patched immediately
Nessus plugins are updated daily

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exploit known vulnerabilities in public-facing applications (T1190) to gain initial access — the same vulnerabilities that scanners identify. Attackers actively scan for unpatched systems using tools like Nmap, Shodan, and custom exploit scanners.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker and the vulnerability scanner are racing for the same vulnerabilities — the scanner finds them to patch, the attacker finds them to exploit. Unpatched vulnerabilities (especially those in CISA KEV) are prime targets. The attacker knows that organizations with poor vulnerability management are easy prey. A well-managed vulnerability program that patches CISA KEV vulnerabilities within days closes the attacker's easiest entry points.
bypass_attempts: Exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities not yet in scanner databases
Targeting systems not included in vulnerability scans (shadow IT, forgotten servers, IoT devices)
Exploiting vulnerabilities in custom applications that generic vulnerability scanners cannot assess

drills: Run Nessus or OpenVAS against a lab environment (like Metasploitable 2/3) and document all findings — classify by CVSS severity and create a remediation plan
Cross-reference scan results with the CISA KEV catalog — identify which discovered vulnerabilities are actively exploited
common_mistakes: Running only unauthenticated scans — missing the majority of vulnerabilities
Not prioritizing remediation by exploitability — patching CVSS 9.0 with no exploit before CVSS 7.0 in CISA KEV
Scanning infrequently — vulnerabilities discovered between scans represent unmonitored risk windows

topics.title: CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs
concepts: CIS Benchmarks: consensus-based secure configuration guidelines for OS, cloud platforms, applications, and network devices — published by the Center for Internet Security
CIS Benchmarks include two levels: Level 1 (basic security, minimal impact) and Level 2 (high security, may impact functionality)
DISA STIGs (Security Technical Implementation Guides): US DoD security configuration standards — more stringent than CIS Benchmarks, mandatory for DoD systems
CIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool): automated tool for scanning against CIS Benchmarks
STIG Viewer: tool for viewing and managing STIG compliance requirements
SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol): NIST standard for automating vulnerability checking and compliance measurement
key_facts: CIS Benchmarks cover 100+ technologies including Windows, Linux, macOS, AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, and web browsers
DISA STIGs are more prescriptive than CIS Benchmarks — they define exact settings with exact values
CIS Level 1 Benchmark for Windows Server includes ~200+ individual configuration checks
Hardening reduces attack surface significantly — disabling unnecessary services, removing default accounts, enforcing strong passwords
SCAP-compliant tools (OpenSCAP, OvalDI) can automate compliance checking against CIS Benchmarks and STIGs

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exploit weak configurations: default passwords (brute force, T1110), unnecessary services running (exploitable attack surface), excessive user privileges (privilege escalation), and missing audit logging. CIS Benchmarks and STIGs close these gaps.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: An unhardened system is an easy target — default configurations are designed for usability, not security. Default services, weak password policies, unnecessary open ports, and excessive privileges all provide attacker footholds. A hardened system (CIS/STIG compliant) removes these low-hanging fruit, forcing the attacker to work harder for initial access.
bypass_attempts: Targeting systems or services not covered by the hardening baseline
Exploiting hardening gaps in the framework itself (new CVEs in hardened configurations)
Using stolen valid credentials — hardening makes brute-force harder but doesn't prevent credential theft

drills: Apply CIS Benchmark Level 1 for Windows Server to a lab system — document changes and scan with CIS-CAT before and after
Compare a specific control between CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG (e.g., password policy) — document the differences
common_mistakes: Applying hardening blindly without testing — some CIS/STIG settings can break applications
Not re-scanning periodically — configuration drift causes systems to fall out of compliance
Only hardening servers and neglecting endpoints (workstations, laptops)

topics.title: Patch Management and Remediation Prioritization
concepts: Patch management lifecycle: discover assets → assess vulnerabilities → prioritize patches → test → deploy → verify → monitor for new vulnerabilities
Prioritization factors: CVSS score, EPSS (exploit probability), CISA KEV status, asset criticality, exposure (internet-facing vs. internal), threat intelligence
Risk-based vulnerability management (RBVM): prioritize based on actual risk rather than just CVSS score
Patch deployment tools: Microsoft SCCM/MECM, WSUS, Ansible, Chef, Puppet, Jamf (macOS), AWS Systems Manager, Azure Update Manager
Virtual patching: deploying WAF rules, IPS signatures, or network ACLs to block exploitation before the patch is deployed
key_facts: A CVSS 7.0 vulnerability on an internet-facing web server in CISA KEV should be patched before a CVSS 9.5 on an isolated internal test server
Average time to patch: organizations typically take 30-60 days for critical vulnerabilities; attackers exploit within days of disclosure
Virtual patching (WAF rules, IPS signatures) buys time between vulnerability disclosure and patch deployment
Patch compliance metrics: percentage of systems patched within SLA (Critical: 7 days, High: 30 days, Medium: 90 days)

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities (T1190) faster than organizations can patch — the time between CVE disclosure and patch deployment is the attacker's window of opportunity.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: When a new CVE is disclosed (especially with a public PoC exploit), the attacker races to exploit it before organizations patch. The defender's patch management speed directly determines how long this window stays open. A mature patch management program that deploys critical patches within days closes the window quickly. The attacker monitors security disclosures and weaponizes exploits within hours.
bypass_attempts: Developing exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities before any patch exists
Targeting systems that cannot be patched quickly (legacy systems, OT/ICS, medical devices)
Exploiting vulnerabilities in the patching infrastructure itself (compromising WSUS or SCCM)

drills: Create a vulnerability remediation priority matrix: take 20 vulnerabilities from a Nessus scan and rank them by actual risk using CVSS + EPSS + CISA KEV + asset criticality
Design a virtual patching workflow: when a critical CVE is disclosed, immediately deploy a WAF rule or IPS signature as interim protection
common_mistakes: Patching by CVSS score alone without considering exploitability (EPSS) and active exploitation (CISA KEV)
Not testing patches before deployment — a bad patch can cause more outage than the vulnerability
Ignoring unpatchable systems (legacy OS, embedded devices) — these require compensating controls

modules.title: Cloud Security Monitoring and CSPM
modules.objective: Monitor cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP) for threats, implement CSPM for continuous compliance, and detect cloud-specific attack patterns.

topics.title: AWS Security Monitoring: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and Config
concepts: AWS CloudTrail: logs all API calls made in the AWS account — the primary audit log for AWS
Amazon GuardDuty: managed threat detection service analyzing CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs using ML and threat intelligence
AWS Config: tracks configuration changes to AWS resources — enables compliance monitoring and drift detection
AWS Security Hub: centralized security findings aggregator — collects from GuardDuty, Config, IAM Access Analyzer, and third-party tools
Key AWS log sources: CloudTrail (management events, data events), VPC Flow Logs, S3 access logs, Route 53 DNS logs
key_facts: CloudTrail logs every API call including source IP, identity (IAM user/role), request parameters, and response
GuardDuty finding types: UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration, DefenseEvasion:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled, Persistence:IAMUser/BackdoorUser
CloudTrail should be enabled for all regions and log file integrity validation should be enabled
AWS Config rules can automatically detect non-compliant resources (public S3 buckets, overly permissive security groups)
IAM users with administrative privileges who have never been used are prime targets for attackers

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers compromise cloud accounts (T1078.004 Cloud Accounts) by stealing IAM credentials via phishing, GitHub leaks, or SSRF. Once in, they enumerate resources, create backdoor users, disable logging (CloudTrail), and exfiltrate data from S3 buckets (T1530).
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: In the cloud, every action is an API call — and every API call is logged by CloudTrail. The attacker cannot operate 'silently' in AWS unless they disable CloudTrail (which itself is a GuardDuty finding: DefenseEvasion:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled). The attacker must either accept full visibility or disable logging (creating an immediate alert).
bypass_attempts: Disabling CloudTrail logging to operate without audit trail (triggers GuardDuty DefenseEvasion finding)
Using the AWS CLI from within a compromised EC2 instance to blend with legitimate instance activity
Creating new IAM users with admin privileges rather than modifying existing ones
Exfiltrating data via legitimate AWS services (sharing S3 buckets with attacker-controlled account)

drills: Enable CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and Config on an AWS account. Simulate an attack (create backdoor IAM user, make S3 bucket public, download large file) and review the resulting CloudTrail events and GuardDuty findings
Write a CloudTrail analysis query (in Athena or Sentinel) to detect IAM users making API calls from new geographic regions
common_mistakes: Not enabling CloudTrail in all regions — attackers operate in regions you're not monitoring
Only logging CloudTrail management events and not data events (GetObject, PutObject) — missing S3 data access
Not setting up alerts for CloudTrail being disabled — attackers disable logging as a first step

topics.title: Azure and GCP Security Monitoring
concepts: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Azure Security Center): unified cloud security posture management and threat protection for Azure
Azure Activity Log: logs all control-plane activities (create/update/delete resources) — Azure equivalent of AWS CloudTrail
Azure Monitor / Log Analytics: centralized logging and monitoring — Sentinel ingests from Log Analytics workspace
Google Cloud Security Command Center (SCC): GCP's security posture and threat detection platform
GCP Cloud Audit Logs: Admin Activity logs and Data Access logs — GCP equivalent of CloudTrail
Microsoft Sentinel: cloud-native SIEM built on Azure — native integration with Microsoft 365, Azure, and hybrid environments
key_facts: Azure Activity Log captures all write operations (control plane) by default; Data Access logs require explicit enablement
Defender for Cloud includes both CSPM (posture management) and workload protection (CWP) for Azure VMs, containers, and databases
Sentinel provides pre-built analytics rules for common Azure attack patterns (impossible travel, brute force, suspicious resource creation)
GCP SCC findings include misconfigurations (public storage), vulnerabilities, and threat detections
All three clouds (AWS, Azure, GCP) use identity-based access (IAM) — monitoring for IAM abuse is universal

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers escalate privileges in cloud environments by abusing IAM misconfigurations — over-privileged roles, unused access keys, and publicly exposed service account keys (T1078.004 Cloud Accounts).
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: Cloud privilege escalation is fundamentally different from on-prem — there are no 'local admin' accounts to exploit. Instead, the attacker abuses IAM policy chains: assuming a role that has more permissions, using a leaked service account key, or exploiting a misconfigured trust policy. The defender monitors for unusual IAM activity.
bypass_attempts: Creating new access keys for existing service accounts rather than using compromised credentials — looks like legitimate key rotation
Abusing existing over-privileged roles rather than escalating — if a role already has admin access, no escalation is needed
Using cloud-native services (Lambda, Cloud Functions) to proxy actions through legitimate compute resources

drills: In Azure, enable Defender for Cloud and review security recommendations. Create a Sentinel analytics rule to detect when a user is added to the Global Administrator role outside business hours
In GCP, enable Security Command Center and review findings. Write a query to detect service account key creation events in Cloud Audit Logs
common_mistakes: Not correlating cloud logs with on-premises logs — hybrid environments have blind spots at the boundary
Not monitoring for unused IAM credentials — stale access keys and service accounts are prime targets
Over-relying on cloud provider security tools without supplementing with independent monitoring (SIEM, third-party CSPM)

topics.title: CSPM, CWPP, and CNAPP
concepts: CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management): continuous assessment of cloud infrastructure for misconfigurations, compliance violations, and security risks — examples: Prisma Cloud, Wiz, Check Point CloudGuard, Lacework
CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform): runtime protection for cloud workloads (VMs, containers, serverless) — vulnerability scanning, runtime threat detection
CIEM (Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management): analysis and management of cloud identity and access permissions — identifies over-privileged users, roles, and service accounts
CNAPP (Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform): unified platform combining CSPM + CWPP + CIEM
Common cloud misconfigurations: public S3 buckets, overly permissive security groups (0.0.0.0/0), exposed databases, disabled encryption, hardcoded credentials in code/IaC
key_facts: Misconfigurations are the #1 cause of cloud breaches — not vulnerabilities or zero-days, but simple configuration errors
Wiz is currently the leading CNAPP platform — providing agentless scanning for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposed secrets, and excessive permissions
CSPM should scan Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform, CloudFormation) BEFORE deployment — 'shift-left' security
CIEM is critical because cloud environments accumulate permission debt over time — roles are granted permissions but rarely revoked
Container security is a key CNAPP capability — scanning container images, runtime drift detection, Kubernetes configuration validation

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers scan for cloud misconfigurations (public S3 buckets, exposed databases, leaked credentials in public repos) using tools like Shodan, GrayhatWarfare, and truffleHog — CSPM continuously monitors for and remediates these exposures.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The cloud attacker's reconnaissance is often external and automated — scanning the entire internet for misconfigured cloud resources. A public S3 bucket, an exposed Elasticsearch cluster, or credentials in a public GitHub repo are all easily found by automated scanners. CSPM tools continuously monitor for these exposures and alert/remediate before attackers find them.
bypass_attempts: Exploiting misconfigurations that CSPM doesn't check for (custom or novel misconfigurations)
Timing attacks between CSPM scan intervals — exploiting a misconfiguration before the next scan detects it
Compromising legitimate credentials to access resources that appear properly secured from the outside

drills: Deploy a CSPM tool (Wiz trial, Prisma Cloud trial, or Prowler open-source for AWS) and scan a cloud environment — document all findings and create a remediation plan
Run Prowler (open-source AWS security assessment tool) against an AWS account and review the compliance checks against CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
common_mistakes: Deploying CSPM in alert-only mode without automated remediation — misconfigurations persist until manually fixed
Not scanning Infrastructure-as-Code before deployment — catching misconfigurations after they're in production is too late
Ignoring CIEM findings — over-privileged identities are as dangerous as misconfigured resources

topics.title: Container and Kubernetes Security Monitoring
concepts: Container image scanning: scanning Docker/OCI images for OS package vulnerabilities, application library vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets, and misconfigurations before deployment
Kubernetes audit logging: kube-apiserver audit log records all API requests to the Kubernetes control plane — the primary security log for K8s
Runtime container security: monitoring running containers for anomalous behavior (unexpected process execution, network connections, file system changes)
Key Kubernetes security controls: RBAC, Network Policies (microsegmentation), Pod Security Standards, Secrets management
Tools: Falco (CNCF runtime security), Aqua Security, Sysdig Secure, kube-bench (CIS Kubernetes Benchmark), Trivy (image scanning)
key_facts: Falco is the CNCF graduated project for container runtime security — uses rules to detect anomalous container behavior in real-time
kube-bench checks Kubernetes cluster configuration against CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
Trivy is a popular open-source vulnerability scanner for container images, file systems, and Kubernetes
Kubernetes RBAC is the primary access control mechanism — over-privileged service accounts are a common attack vector
Container escape (breaking out of the container to the host) is a high-severity finding

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers exploit container escape vulnerabilities (T1611 Escape to Host) to break from a container to the underlying host, gaining access to all containers on the node. They may also implant malicious container images (T1525 Implant Internal Image) in registries.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: Container environments present a unique attack surface — a single container escape can compromise the entire host node and all containers running on it. The attacker's goals are: escape the container to the host, access other containers, pivot to the Kubernetes API server, access secrets. Runtime security tools (Falco) and image scanning (Trivy) are the defender's primary countermeasures.
bypass_attempts: Exploiting zero-day container escape vulnerabilities that runtime security tools don't yet detect
Operating within the container's normal behavior profile to avoid triggering Falco rules
Compromising the container image supply chain — injecting malicious code into base images or CI/CD pipelines

drills: Scan a Docker image with Trivy: trivy image nginx:latest — document all vulnerabilities and identify which are fixable
Install Falco on a Kubernetes cluster and review the default rules — simulate a container opening a shell (kubectl exec) and verify Falco detects it
common_mistakes: Scanning images at build time but not enforcing that only scanned images can be deployed (admission control)
Not monitoring Kubernetes audit logs — the API server is the control plane for the entire cluster
Granting excessive RBAC permissions to service accounts — following least privilege is critical

modules.title: Cyber Threat Intelligence
modules.objective: Integrate threat intelligence into defensive operations using STIX/TAXII, MISP, and intelligence-driven hunting to proactively detect emerging threats.

topics.title: CTI Lifecycle and Intelligence Types
concepts: CTI lifecycle: (1) Requirements/Planning → (2) Collection → (3) Processing & Exploitation → (4) Analysis & Production → (5) Dissemination → (6) Feedback
Intelligence types: Strategic (high-level trends, threat actor motivations, executive briefings), Operational (specific threats, campaign analysis, TTPs), Tactical (IOCs, hashes, IPs, domains)
Intelligence sources: internal (past incidents, SIEM data, honeypots), external (ISACs/ISAOs, commercial feeds, open-source intelligence, government advisories)
ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers): sector-specific intelligence sharing organizations — FS-ISAC, MS-ISAC, Aviation-ISAC, etc.
Threat actor attribution: tracking threat groups (APTs, cybercriminal groups) by TTPs, infrastructure, and objectives — MITRE ATT&CK groups
key_facts: The CTI lifecycle is circular — feedback from intelligence consumers (SOC, IR) drives new collection requirements
Tactical intelligence (IOCs) has the shortest lifespan — IPs, domains, and hashes change frequently. TTPs have the longest lifespan.
ISACs are a critical source of sector-specific threat intelligence — many provide free STIX/TAXII feeds to member organizations
Intelligence requirements should be specific and aligned with business risk: 'What TTPs are threat groups targeting financial services using?'

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers themselves conduct reconnaissance (T1592 Gather Victim Host Information) before attacking — CTI flips this by gathering intelligence on the attackers: their TTPs, infrastructure, tools, and objectives.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker operates under the assumption that the defender doesn't know who they are or how they operate. CTI disrupts this assumption — by tracking threat groups, their TTPs, and infrastructure, the defender can anticipate attacks before they happen. When a defender has good CTI, they can proactively hunt for specific threat groups' techniques and block known infrastructure.
bypass_attempts: Rapidly rotating infrastructure, tools, and TTPs to avoid being tracked and attributed
Operating as a new, unattributed threat group with no historical intelligence footprint
Deliberately planting false flags to mislead intelligence analysis

drills: Write intelligence requirements for a fictional organization (e.g., a hospital): identify the top 3 threat groups likely to target them and what TTPs to watch for
Subscribe to a free threat intelligence feed (CISA advisories, MS-ISAC) and integrate 10 IOCs into your SIEM as watchlists
common_mistakes: Collecting intelligence without defined requirements — gathering IOCs and reports that are never used
Treating all IOCs equally — a domain from 3 years ago is not actionable, but a hash from yesterday is
Not sharing intelligence back to the community — intelligence sharing is reciprocal

topics.title: STIX, TAXII, MISP, and OpenCTI
concepts: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression): standardized JSON-based language for representing cyber threat intelligence — describes indicators, observables, TTPs, threat actors, campaigns, and relationships
TAXII (Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information): HTTPS-based transport protocol for sharing STIX content between organizations and tools
MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform): open-source threat intelligence platform for collecting, storing, distributing, and sharing threat intelligence — supports STIX import/export
OpenCTI: open-source threat intelligence platform with a graph-based data model — integrates with STIX 2.x natively
Intelligence platforms vs. feeds: platforms (MISP, OpenCTI, ThreatConnect, Anomali) manage, enrich, and correlate intelligence; feeds provide raw indicators
key_facts: STIX 2.x uses JSON-LD format and defines objects: Indicator, Observed Data, Attack Pattern, Threat Actor, Intrusion Set, Malware, Tool, Campaign, Identity, Relationship, Report
MISP is the most widely deployed open-source threat intelligence platform — used by ISACs, CSIRTs, and commercial organizations worldwide
TAXII defines collections and channels for intelligence sharing — a TAXII server hosts collections that clients can poll or subscribe to
MISP 'galaxies' provide structured taxonomies for classification: MITRE ATT&CK, threat actors, ransomware, sectors
OpenCTI's graph model visualizes relationships between threat actors, campaigns, TTPs, and indicators

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers use shared infrastructure, tools, and TTPs across multiple campaigns — CTI platforms (MISP, OpenCTI) correlate these across organizations, identifying shared infrastructure that links disparate attacks to the same threat group.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's infrastructure (C2 domains, IPs, certificates) is their fingerprint across campaigns. When multiple organizations share observations via STIX/TAXII/MISP, the defender community can link attacks that the attacker intended to appear separate. The attacker must invest in entirely new infrastructure for each campaign to avoid this correlation.
bypass_attempts: Using completely separate infrastructure for each campaign — no shared C2 domains, IPs, or certificates
Compromising legitimate infrastructure (websites, cloud services) for C2 to avoid attribution
Rapidly cycling through disposable infrastructure (burner domains, short-lived cloud instances)

drills: Install MISP (Docker) and import a threat intelligence feed (e.g., CISA, abuse.ch) — explore the imported indicators and use MISP galaxies to classify them by ATT&CK technique
Set up a TAXII client to pull indicators from a public feed and ingest them into your SIEM as watchlists
common_mistakes: Not enriching raw IOCs with context before use — an IP address without context (what threat group, what campaign, what TTP) is barely actionable
Not aging out stale indicators — 3-year-old IPs in a blocklist generate false positives and reduce trust in the intelligence
Not correlating intelligence with internal telemetry — external IOCs should be matched against SIEM data, not just added to blocklists

topics.title: Diamond Model and Pyramid of Pain
concepts: Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis (Sergio Caltagirone, Andrew Pendergast, Chris Betz, 2013): every intrusion event has 4 core features — Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim — connected by relationships
Diamond Model axioms: every intrusion contains these 4 features; the defender can pivot from any feature to discover the others
Pyramid of Pain (David Bianco): the hierarchy of indicators from easy to detect but trivial for attacker to change (hashes) up to TTPs (hard to detect but most painful for attacker to change)
Pyramid levels (bottom to top): Hash Values → IP Addresses → Domain Names → Host Artifacts → Network Artifacts → Tools → TTPs
Intelligence-driven defense: use the Diamond Model and Pyramid of Pain to focus defensive efforts on high-value indicators (TTPs) that cause the most pain to attackers
key_facts: Diamond Model pivot: if you find one feature (e.g., a C2 IP address = Infrastructure), you can search for related features (what malware = Capability, what victim = Victim, what adversary = Adversary)
Blocking a hash value causes the attacker almost no pain (trivial to change); detecting their TTPs forces them to retrain and retool (maximum pain)
The Diamond Model was developed at the US DoD and published in 2013 as a foundational CTI analysis framework
Pyramid of Pain drives prioritization: invest detection and hunting effort in the upper layers (network/host artifacts, tools, TTPs) for maximum impact
Both frameworks are complementary — Diamond Model for analysis/understanding, Pyramid of Pain for prioritization

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers use reusable infrastructure, tools, and TTPs across campaigns — the Diamond Model and Pyramid of Pain help defenders identify and exploit these reuses, pivoting from one observable to map the attacker's full infrastructure and capabilities.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's efficiency is their vulnerability: reusing infrastructure, tools, and TTPs saves them time and money but creates correlations that CTI analysis can exploit. When the defender operates at the TTP level (top of the Pyramid of Pain), the attacker must fundamentally change their approach — developing new techniques, training operators, and building new infrastructure. This is the most expensive outcome for the attacker.
bypass_attempts: Complete operational separation between campaigns — new infrastructure, new tools, new techniques for each operation (maximum cost)
Deploying false flags and misleading indicators to corrupt the defender's Diamond Model analysis
Rapidly evolving TTPs to stay ahead of defender intelligence faster than it can be shared

drills: Take a real-world intrusion (from The DFIR Report or a CISA advisory) and map it using the Diamond Model: identify Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim, and the relationships between them
Take 5 IOCs from a threat report and place them on the Pyramid of Pain — rank them by how much pain each causes the attacker if detected and blocked
common_mistakes: Focusing intelligence efforts on the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain (hashes, IPs) — high volume, low impact
Not using the Diamond Model to pivot from known indicators to discover unknown infrastructure and capabilities
Treating CTI as a feed-consumption exercise rather than an analytical discipline

modules.title: Zero Trust Architecture
modules.objective: Design and implement Zero Trust principles per NIST SP 800-207, including identity-centric access, microsegmentation, and continuous verification.

topics.title: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Principles
concepts: Zero Trust core assumption: 'Never trust, always verify' — no implicit trust based on network location; all access requests must be authenticated, authorized, and continuously validated
NIST SP 800-207 defines 7 basic tenets of Zero Trust
Tenet 1: All data sources and computing services are considered resources
Tenet 2: All communication is secured regardless of network location
Tenet 3: Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis
Tenet 4: Access is determined by dynamic policy including identity, application/service, and security posture
Tenet 5: The enterprise monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of all owned and associated assets
Tenet 6: All resource authentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed
Tenet 7: The enterprise collects as much information as possible about the current state of assets, network infrastructure, and communications to improve its security posture
key_facts: Zero Trust shifts security from network-perimeter-based to identity-and-context-based
NIST SP 800-207 was published in August 2020 and is the authoritative Zero Trust reference
The traditional 'castle-and-moat' model assumes trusted internal network — Zero Trust assumes breach
CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model defines 5 pillars: Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications & Workloads, Data
Zero Trust is a journey, not a product — it requires process, culture, and technology changes

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers rely on lateral movement (T1021 Remote Services) and stolen valid credentials (T1078 Valid Accounts) once inside the network — in a traditional network, reaching the internal network means trusted access to everything. Zero Trust eliminates this trust, requiring authentication and authorization for every resource access.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: In a Zero Trust environment, the attacker who compromises one system cannot pivot freely to others — every lateral movement attempt requires fresh authentication, is evaluated against dynamic policy, and is logged with full context. The attacker's traditional advantage (once inside, everything is reachable) is removed. Every resource access becomes a potential detection point.
bypass_attempts: Compromising the Zero Trust policy engine or identity provider (IdP) to modify access policies
Stealing valid tokens/credentials that pass the continuous verification checks
Exploiting trust relationships between the identity provider and service providers (federation attacks)

drills: Map your organization's current security architecture against the 7 NIST SP 800-207 tenets — identify which tenets are fully implemented, partially implemented, or not implemented
Assess your organization's Zero Trust maturity using the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model (5 pillars x 4 maturity levels: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal)
common_mistakes: Treating Zero Trust as a single product purchase (e.g., 'we bought a ZTNA solution so we have Zero Trust') — it requires holistic architecture changes
Only implementing Zero Trust for remote access (ZTNA) while leaving internal network flat and unsegmented
Not continuously validating trust — session-based access that persists indefinitely defeats the purpose

topics.title: Microsegmentation and Network Controls
concepts: Microsegmentation: dividing the network into granular security zones, each with its own access controls — limits lateral movement by restricting east-west traffic flows
Traditional segmentation: VLANs and subnet-level firewalls (coarse); Microsegmentation: per-workload, per-process, per-identity rules (fine-grained)
Implementation approaches: network-based (ACLs, firewalls, VXLAN), host-based (host firewalls, EDR-enforced), identity-based (ZTNA, software-defined perimeter)
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enables dynamic microsegmentation — policies follow the workload regardless of network location
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA): replaces VPN with identity-and-context-aware access to specific applications, not the entire network
key_facts: CISA published 'Zero Trust Maturity Model' and microsegmentation guidance in 2025 emphasizing it as a core Zero Trust control
Microsegmentation limits the blast radius of a compromise — even if an attacker reaches one segment, they cannot pivot to others
Effective microsegmentation requires asset discovery, dependency mapping, and policy modeling before enforcement — understand the application flows first
ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) products: Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, Palo Alto Prisma Access, Microsoft Entra Private Access
Microsegmentation is the network-layer implementation of least privilege — default deny, allow only explicitly needed flows

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers move laterally using remote services (T1021) and lateral tool transfer (T1570) — microsegmentation blocks these movements by enforcing default-deny between segments, requiring explicit policy for any cross-segment communication.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: In a microsegmented environment, the attacker who compromises a web server cannot directly access the database server — there is no network path between them unless explicitly allowed. Every lateral movement attempt either fails (blocked) or generates a policy violation alert (if the segment allows logging of denied flows). The attacker must find application-level paths that the segmentation policy permits, or find a way to modify the segmentation policy itself.
bypass_attempts: Finding permitted paths between segments (e.g., through an application API that spans segments)
Compromising the microsegmentation controller or policy engine to create allowed paths
Using out-of-band communication channels (e.g., cloud metadata service, management interfaces) that bypass segmentation rules

drills: Map your organization's east-west traffic flows and identify which flows are necessary (application dependencies) vs. unnecessary (potential lateral movement paths)
Design a microsegmentation policy for a 3-tier web application: web tier → app tier → database tier, with default-deny between tiers except explicitly required ports/protocols
common_mistakes: Implementing microsegmentation without understanding application dependencies — blocking legitimate traffic and causing outages
Starting with enforcement instead of monitoring — always run in monitor-only mode first to validate policies
Making segmentation rules too broad — 'allow all from web subnet to app subnet' defeats the purpose of microsegmentation

topics.title: Identity-Centric Security and Continuous Authentication
concepts: Identity as the new perimeter: in Zero Trust, identity (not network location) determines access — every request is authenticated and authorized based on user identity, device posture, and context
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): requires multiple authentication factors (something you know, have, are) — foundational Zero Trust control
Conditional Access: dynamic access policies based on real-time context (user location, device compliance, risk score, time of day, resource sensitivity)
Continuous authentication: re-validating user identity throughout the session, not just at login — detects session hijacking and insider threats
Identity Provider (IdP) and Single Sign-On (SSO): centralized identity management — Okta, Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), PingIdentity, Google Workspace Identity
key_facts: MFA blocks >99.9% of automated account compromise attacks (Microsoft security research)
Conditional Access evaluates signals: user risk, sign-in risk, device compliance, location, and application sensitivity before granting access
Passwordless authentication (FIDO2/WebAuthn, Windows Hello, smart cards) eliminates the password attack surface entirely
Privileged Access Management (PAM): just-in-time, just-enough access for admin accounts — CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Microsoft Entra PIM
Identity Governance and Administration (IGA): managing the identity lifecycle (joiner-mover-leaver), access reviews, and segregation of duties

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers use stolen valid credentials (T1078) or brute force (T1110) to gain access — identity-centric security (MFA, conditional access, PAM) blocks these attacks by requiring additional verification factors and evaluating access context in real-time.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: In an identity-centric environment, the attacker who steals a password cannot access resources — MFA requires a second factor, conditional access evaluates the request context (new device? unusual location? suspicious time?), and PAM limits admin access to just-in-time windows. The attacker's stolen credential is insufficient. They must steal the MFA token, compromise the device (for device-based conditional access), or bypass the identity provider entirely.
bypass_attempts: Stealing MFA tokens via adversarial-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing (e.g., Evilginx2)
Registering a new MFA device after compromising the account (MFA fatigue/push bombing)
Exploiting the identity provider directly (Golden SAML, AD CS attacks)
Using pass-the-cookie or token theft to bypass MFA for already-authenticated sessions

drills: Implement Conditional Access policies in Azure AD / Entra ID: require MFA for all users, block access from non-compliant devices, require password change for high-risk sign-ins
Design a PAM workflow: admin requests just-in-time access to a privileged role → approval workflow → time-limited access (4 hours) → automatic revocation → full audit trail
common_mistakes: Implementing MFA without protecting against AiTM phishing (use phishing-resistant MFA like FIDO2)
Not applying conditional access to all applications (legacy apps may bypass the policy)
Standing admin privileges (always-on admin accounts) instead of just-in-time access — violates least privilege

modules.title: Deception Technology and Honeypots
modules.objective: Deploy deception technologies (honeypots, canary tokens, honeyfiles) to detect attackers early in the kill chain with high-fidelity alerts.

topics.title: Honeypot Concepts and Deployment
concepts: Honeypot: a decoy system designed to attract attackers, study their behavior, and generate high-fidelity alerts — no legitimate user should ever interact with a honeypot

Honeypot types: low-interaction (simulated services, e.g., Honeyd, Cowrie), high-interaction (real OS/services, e.g., real VMs deployed as decoys), research honeypots (for threat intelligence gathering), production honeypots (for early warning detection)
Honeynet: a network of honeypots designed to present a realistic target environment
Honeywall/honeynet gateway: controls and monitors traffic in/out of the honeypot environment
Deployment considerations: realism (must blend with production environment), placement (within production network segments), alerting (immediate notification on any interaction)
key_facts: Honeypot alerts have extremely high fidelity — any interaction with a honeypot is suspicious by definition because no legitimate user should access it
Cowrie is a popular open-source SSH/Telnet honeypot — medium-interaction that logs commands, captures malware payloads, and records attacker sessions
T-Pot is an all-in-one honeypot platform from Telekom Security — bundles multiple honeypots (Cowrie, Dionaea, Honeypy, ConPot, etc.) with ELK for analysis
High-interaction honeypots provide the richest intelligence but carry risk — the attacker could use them as a pivot point
Honeypots are especially effective for detecting internal lateral movement — if an attacker reaches an internal honeypot, they are already inside the network

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers perform network scanning and discovery (T1046 Network Service Discovery) and lateral movement (T1021 Remote Services) — if they scan or access a honeypot, the interaction is immediately detected because no legitimate user should ever touch it.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker cannot distinguish a honeypot from a real system — if it looks like a vulnerable SSH server, they will attempt to exploit it. The moment they connect, the defender knows an attacker is in the network. Unlike traditional alerts that may be false positives, honeypot alerts are almost always true positives. The attacker's scanning and exploitation behaviors betray their presence.
bypass_attempts: Fingerprinting honeypots by probing for simulation artifacts (low-interaction honeypots have telltale signs)
Avoiding honeypots by using intelligence about common honeypot deployments and configurations
Using the honeypot itself as a pivot while being careful not to trigger alerts (exploiting but not modifying)

drills: Deploy Cowrie SSH honeypot (or T-Pot) in an isolated lab network — observe attacker connections, brute-force attempts, and command execution. Document the TTPs used by attackers
Deploy an internal honeypot (fake SMB share, fake web server) within a production network segment — any connection to it is an immediate high-fidelity alert
common_mistakes: Deploying honeypots that are too obvious — attackers fingerprint and avoid them, wasting the deployment
Not isolating high-interaction honeypots — attackers can use them as pivots to attack real systems
Not monitoring honeypot alerts — a honeypot that nobody watches is worse than useless because it wastes resources

topics.title: Canary Tokens and Honeyfiles
concepts: Canary token: a lightweight tripwire embedded in files, folders, URLs, database records, or API keys that generates an alert when accessed — Thinkst Canary (canarytokens.org) is the most popular free tool
Canary token types: fake AWS API keys, fake SQL database credentials, Word/Excel documents with embedded beacons, fake credit card numbers, DNS canary tokens
Honeyfile: a decoy file placed in a location that an attacker is likely to access (e.g., 'passwords.docx' in a file share) — opening the file triggers an alert
Honey credentials: fake credentials planted in code, configuration files, or password managers — if used for authentication, they trigger an alert
Honey data: decoy database records, API endpoints, or administrative interfaces that alert on access
key_facts: Canary tokens from Thinkst Canary (canarytokens.org) are free and deploy in seconds — they generate DNS or HTTP callbacks when triggered
Canary tokens have near-zero false positive rate — only an attacker (or someone exploring where they shouldn't) would access them
Fake AWS API keys as canary tokens: if planted in a code repository and someone uses them, AWS API calls trigger an alert — detects credential theft from public or private repos
Honeyfiles should have enticing names ('financial_data.xlsx', 'admin_passwords.txt', 'database_backup.sql') to attract attacker attention
Canary tokens work because they exploit attacker behavior — attackers enumerate, explore, and steal everything they find; canary tokens are designed to be found and accessed

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers search for unsecured credentials (T1552 Unsecured Credentials) and collect data from target systems (T1005 Data from Local System) — honey credentials and honeyfiles are designed to be found and accessed by attackers, triggering immediate alerts.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's instinct to collect everything they find is their vulnerability — they cannot resist opening a file named 'passwords.txt' or using credentials found in a config file. Canary tokens exploit this greed. When the attacker accesses the honeyfile or uses the honey credentials, the defender receives an immediate high-fidelity alert. The attacker doesn't know which credentials are real vs. honey until they try them — by then, it's too late.
bypass_attempts: Fingerprinting honeyfiles and canary tokens before accessing them (checking for tracking beacons)
Avoiding files and credentials that look 'too good to be true'
Using obtained credentials only from infrastructure that doesn't callback to known canary token endpoints

drills: Generate canary tokens at canarytokens.org (fake AWS keys, fake SQL creds, Word doc tokens) and deploy them in strategic locations: code repositories, file shares, password managers, configuration files
Create honeyfiles with enticing names ('passwords.xlsx', 'salary_data.xlsx') in file shares — configure file access auditing to alert immediately when opened
common_mistakes: Not deploying enough canary tokens — a few tokens may be missed by an attacker; widespread deployment increases detection probability
Making canary tokens too obvious — if the honeyfile or honey credential looks unrealistic, the attacker may skip it
Not monitoring canary token alerts — a triggered canary token that goes unnoticed is a wasted opportunity

topics.title: Deception Across the Attack Lifecycle
concepts: Deception at each kill chain stage: Reconnaissance (honeypot services that attract scanning), Initial Access (fake login portals that capture attacker credentials), Execution (canary commands/scripts that alert when run), Persistence (fake persistence locations that alert when modified), Lateral Movement (fake hosts/services/credentials that detect probing), Data Exfiltration (honey data that alerts when exfiltrated)
Deception architecture: distributed decoys + centralized management + SIEM integration — commercial platforms (Attivo/SentinelOne, Acalvio, TrapX, Hexis) provide enterprise-scale deception

Early warning value: deception provides the earliest possible detection because it doesn't wait for the attacker to trigger a signature or threshold — any interaction with a decoy is immediately suspicious
Deception as a force multiplier: a few well-placed decoys can protect an entire network — the attacker doesn't know which systems are real and which are decoys
Intelligence gathering: high-interaction honeypots capture attacker tools, techniques, and infrastructure — valuable threat intelligence
key_facts: Deception provides the highest signal-to-noise ratio of any detection technology — near-zero false positives because legitimate users don't interact with decoys
Commercial deception platforms can auto-deploy decoys that match the production environment (same OS, same services, same naming conventions) for realism
Deception is particularly effective against insider threats — an employee accessing honeyfiles or honey credentials is immediately suspicious
Deception complements (not replaces) traditional detection — use alongside SIEM, EDR, and IDS for defense-in-depth

offense_pairing.what_red_does: Attackers operate across the full kill chain: scanning for services, searching for credentials, collecting data, moving laterally. Deception technology places traps at each stage — decoy services for scanners, honey credentials for credential thieves, honeyfiles for data collectors, fake hosts for lateral movers.
offense_pairing.attacker_perspective: The attacker's biggest enemy in a deception-rich environment is uncertainty: they cannot trust any system, credential, or file. Every action could trigger an alert. This paranoia slows them down and increases operational cost. If they scan a network full of honeypots, they trigger alerts at every step. If they use stolen credentials, they may be using honey credentials that callback. The defender gains asymmetric advantage: cheap decoys that are expensive for the attacker to validate.

Using behavioral analysis to distinguish real from decoy systems

common_mistakes: Deploying deception in isolation — not integrating alerts into the SIEM or SOAR means deception alerts may be missed
Not maintaining deception realism — decoys that don't match the production environment are easily identified and avoided
